lessons.title: Four Gospels, one Christ
lessons.idea: The four Gospels are the heart of all Scripture because they give us the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word. Each evangelist writes for a particular audience with a particular emphasis, yet all four bear witness to the one Christ.
lessons.question: Why four Gospels?
lessons.activity: “Four Gospels at a glance” (30 min). Fill a chart with: author, likely audience, symbol (man, lion, ox, eagle), opening, emphasis (Matthew: Jesus fulfills Israel’s story; Mark: the suffering Servant, action; Luke: mercy and the poor; John: the Word, signs and “I am”). Read the opening lines of each (Matthew 1:1, Mark 1:1, Luke 1:1–4, John 1:1).
teach: The Gospels are “the principal source for the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word, our Savior” (CCC 125; Dei Verbum 18). They hold a special place, which is why we stand to hear them at Mass.

There are four Gospels, not one harmonized account, because the Church wanted to keep the fullness of each witness (CCC 127). Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material (the “Synoptics”); John is distinct.
Each tells a historical story shaped by faith. Luke says he “investigated everything carefully” to give certainty (Luke 1:1–4). The Church affirms their historicity (CCC 126; Dei Verbum 19).
The traditional symbols (Revelation 4:7) are Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, John the eagle.
talk: Why four Gospels instead of one?
How do we know they are reliable?
quiz: The Gospels are…|Fiction|Our principal source for the life of Christ|Poetry|Commentary|1|CCC 125.
The first Gospel written is generally held to be…|John|Luke|Matthew|Mark|3|Tradition.
The Gospels were formed from…|Dreams|Later councils|Myth|Oral tradition and eyewitnesses|3|CCC 126.
lessons.life: Read the first chapter of each Gospel over four days.
lessons.saint: Mark: Peter’s interpreter, who wrote down the preaching of the apostle.
misc: “The Gospels are biographies in the modern sense.”
“The differences prove the Gospels are false.”
lessons.mem: “These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)
lessons.hook: Show four photographs of the same building from four sides. “Are they different? Are they all true?” Four Gospels are four faithful views of one Lord.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name each Gospel’s focus and one reason the Church keeps four.

script.open: Ask four volunteers to leave the room. Bring them back one by one to hear the same short story from you, then tell it in their own words. Compare the four versions. Say, “Same event, four tellers. Gospels are like this.”
teach: Say: “We have four Gospels, not one. The word ‘Gospel’ means ‘good news.’ The four are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They are not biographies in the modern sense. Each is a portrait of Jesus, written for a particular community to bring them to faith. The Church placed these four in the canon because they come from the apostles’ own preaching and teaching, and she rejected others.”

Say: “Matthew was written for Jewish Christians. He quotes the Old Testament often to show Jesus as the Messiah, a new Moses who gives a new law in the Sermon on the Mount. Mark is the shortest and fastest, showing Jesus as the powerful Son of God who suffers. Luke, writing for Gentiles, stresses mercy, the poor, women, prayer and the Holy Spirit. John is quite different. It begins ‘In the beginning was the Word,’ includes the long discourses and ‘I am’ sayings, and shows Jesus as the divine Son who reveals the Father. Matthew, Mark and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they ‘see together.’”

Say: “Early Christians gave each Gospel a symbol, from Ezekiel and Revelation: Matthew the man (it opens with Jesus’ human ancestry), Mark the lion (the voice in the wilderness), Luke the ox (the sacrificial animal; it opens in the Temple), John the eagle (it soars to the divine heights). We hear one Jesus through four voices. Differences in details do not mean the Gospels are untrustworthy, any more than four witnesses would. They are complementary.”
ask: What does ‘Gospel’ mean? (Good news.)
Which Gospel is for Jewish Christians? (Matthew.)
What are the Synoptic Gospels? (Matthew, Mark and Luke.)
practice: Choose a story told in more than one Gospel, such as the calming of the storm (Mark 4:35-41, Matthew 8:23-27, Luke 8:22-25).
Read the versions in groups and make a chart: what is the same, what differs, what each stresses.
Add one line: “Matthew emphasizes…, Mark…, Luke…”
Discuss why four Gospels are better than one.
script.close: Pray: “Lord Jesus, let us know you through the Gospels.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read one chapter of Mark in one sitting.”

tryit: Compare one story in two Gospels.
List what is the same and what differs.
Say what each Gospel stresses.
lessons.saintStory:
Mark, also called John Mark, appears in the Acts of the Apostles. His mother Mary had a house in Jerusalem where the first Christians prayed. He went with Paul and Barnabas on their first journey, but turned back partway, and Paul was displeased. Later he was reconciled with Paul, and spent years with Peter in Rome, who called him “my son Mark.”
An early Christian writer named Papias said that Mark, as Peter’s interpreter, wrote down accurately what Peter preached about the Lord. This is the Gospel of Mark, the shortest and probably the earliest. It moves fast, and uses the word “immediately” again and again.
Tradition says Mark founded the Church in Alexandria, Egypt, and died there as a martyr. His symbol is the lion.

lessons.title: How the Gospels were formed
lessons.idea: The Gospels came about in three stages: Jesus’ life and teaching, the oral preaching of the apostles, and the writing down by the evangelists. The evangelists selected, arranged and adapted what they received, always remaining faithful to Jesus.
lessons.question: What stages shaped the Gospels?
lessons.activity: “Gospel timeline” (25 min). Create a line: c. AD 30 Jesus’ death and resurrection; 30–50 oral preaching; c. 50–60 Paul’s letters; c. 65–70 Mark; 80–90 Matthew and Luke; c. 90–100 John. Add the three stages. Read Luke 1:1–4 and John 21:24–25 and underline words like “eyewitnesses” and “handed down.”
teach: Three stages (CCC 126; Dei Verbum 19): Jesus’ life and teaching, the apostolic preaching “with that fuller understanding which they enjoyed after being instructed by the glorious events of Christ’s life,” and the written Gospels.

The evangelists “selected certain elements from the many which had been handed on, ... reduced some of them to a synthesis, explained some things in view of the situation of their churches” while keeping the truth of Jesus’ words (CCC 126).
Paul’s letters (written before the Gospels) already hand on core traditions: the Eucharist (1 Corinthians 11:23–26), the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–8).
Comfortable with the human side of the process, remind students that the Spirit guided it (CCC 105–107).
talk: Why were the Gospels written down?
quiz: Luke wrote his Gospel after…|Dreaming|Investigating from the beginning|Reading Mark only|Losing his notes|1|Luke 1:3.
The Gospels reflect…|Eyewitness tradition|Rumor|Pure invention|Greek myth|0|Dei Verbum 19.
John’s Gospel is…|A genealogy|A chronicle|Highly theological|A law code|2|CCC 125.
lessons.life: Read Luke 1:1–4 and note what Luke says about method.
lessons.saint: Luke: the physician and evangelist who investigated everything carefully.
misc: “Nobody wrote anything down until much later, so we can’t trust it.”
“The evangelists made up stories to fit their message.”
lessons.mem: “We did not follow cleverly devised myths... but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.” (2 Peter 1:16)
lessons.hook: Ask a student to retell a story from last week to a friend; then ask the friend to retell it to another. “What changes? What must stay the same?” Introduce how the Gospel was passed on, with careful memory and living witnesses.
lessons.assess: Ask students to place the three stages in order and say why oral tradition mattered.

script.open: Ask, “How do you know what happened at an event you did not attend, like your own baptism? Who told you? What do you trust?” Let them reply. “That’s a bit like how we got the Gospels.”
teach: Read Luke 1:1-4. Say: “Luke tells us how he wrote: from eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, after careful investigation, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught. The Church teaches that the Gospels came about in three stages. First, the life and teaching of Jesus, about AD 30. Second, oral tradition: after the Resurrection, the apostles preached what Jesus had said and done, shaped to their audiences, with a deeper understanding after Easter and Pentecost.”

Say: “Third, the written Gospels. The sacred authors selected from the tradition, put some in a summary form, and adapted the telling to their churches, always keeping the truth about Jesus. Mark is thought to have been written first, around AD 65-70. Matthew and Luke around AD 70-90, and John around 90-100. The Church teaches that the four Gospels ‘faithfully hand on what Jesus the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation, until the day he was taken up.’ (Dei Verbum 19)”

Say: “So the Gospels are historical, though not as modern biographies are. They were written by people who believed in the Resurrection, to bring others to faith. John says, ‘These are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.’ (John 20:31) They have been tested by thousands of ancient manuscripts, far more than for any other ancient text. We can trust what they tell us.”
ask: What are the three stages of Gospel formation? (Jesus’ life, oral tradition, written Gospels.)
Why did Luke write? (So that Theophilus might know the certainty of what he was taught.)
Why were the Gospels written? (To bring people to faith in Jesus.)
practice: Draw a timeline from AD 30 to AD 100.
Mark: Jesus’ ministry, the Resurrection and Pentecost, oral preaching, Mark, Matthew and Luke, John.
Label the three stages in different colors.
Write one sentence: “I can trust the Gospels because…”
script.close: Pray: “Lord, thank you for the witnesses who handed on your word.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Luke 1:1-4 aloud to someone.”

tryit: Put the three stages of Gospel formation in order.
Match each to who was involved.
Read Luke 1:1-4.
lessons.saintStory:
Luke was a Gentile, a physician, and a friend and traveling companion of Paul. Paul mentions him in his letters as “the beloved physician.” Luke joined Paul on part of his journeys, and in Acts the narrator begins to say “we” when Luke is with him.
Luke wrote two books, the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. He begins his Gospel: “Since many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as they were delivered to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account.”
Only Luke tells the stories of the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son and the Annunciation in detail. Tradition says he knew Mary and learned from her, and that he died at eighty-four. He is patron of physicians.

lessons.title: Reading the Gospels well
lessons.idea: The Church gives three guidelines for reading Scripture: attend to the unity of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and respect the analogy of faith. With prayer and in context, the Gospels speak today.
lessons.question: What are the three criteria for interpretation?
lessons.activity: “Three tools” (30 min). Take Luke 24:44–48 and a short passage (e.g., Matthew 16:13–19). Students use the three tools: (1) unity: which Old Testament texts or other Gospel passages relate? (2) Tradition: how have the Fathers or the liturgy read it? (3) analogy of faith: how does it fit with what the Church teaches? Report to the class.
teach: CCC 112–114: be especially attentive to “the content and unity of the whole Scripture,” read it “within the living Tradition of the whole Church,” and be attentive to “the coherence of the truths of faith among themselves” (analogy of faith).
Also ask: who wrote it, to whom, when, and in what literary form (CCC 109–110). Context prevents misuse of single verses.
Prayer matters: “Scripture must be read and interpreted in the sacred spirit in which it was written” (CCC 111). Lectio divina is the Church’s ancient practice.
Show a common misreading (e.g., “do not judge,” Matthew 7:1) and how the three tools correct it.
talk: What is the analogy of faith?
quiz: The analogy of faith is…|A parable|The coherence of the truths of faith|A comparison|A hymn|1|CCC 114.
The Church reads Scripture in light of…|The news|Tradition|Rumor|Opinion only|1|CCC 113.
Which is NOT a criterion?|Private mood|Tradition|Analogy of faith|Unity of Scripture|0|CCC 112-114.
lessons.life: Apply the three criteria to one passage.
lessons.saint: Bede the Venerable: a monk who was finishing his translation of John’s Gospel on the day he died.
misc: “Anyone can interpret the Bible however they feel.”
“Context is a way to explain the Bible away.”
lessons.mem: “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.” (Luke 24:45)
lessons.hook: Show a puzzle with one piece alone. “Does this piece make sense without the picture?” A verse alone can mislead.
lessons.assess: Ask students to use the three tools on a short passage you provide.

script.open: Read a short Gospel passage aloud (for example Mark 10:46-52) and ask, “What did you hear? What did you not notice?” Say, “Reading the Gospels well is a skill. Let’s learn four questions.”
teach: Say: “The Church gives us three guidelines, from Dei Verbum 12. First, read with attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture. A verse must be read in light of the whole Bible, which is one story that leads to Christ. Second, read within the living Tradition of the Church. We read with the Church, who gave us the Bible and knows how it has been understood. Third, be attentive to the analogy of faith, that is, the harmony of the truths of the faith. Scripture cannot teach contrary to the Church’s doctrine.”

Say: “In practice, ask four questions. What does it say? Observe: who, what, where, when. What does it mean? Understand the context and form, and the other Gospels. Where does it point? See how it connects to the Old Testament, to Jesus, and to the sacraments. What does it ask of me? Apply it. This follows a very old way of reading called lectio divina: read, meditate, pray, contemplate. St. Jerome said, ‘Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.’”

Say: “Some cautions. Don’t pull out a verse and use it in a way that contradicts the whole. Don’t read your own ideas into the text. Don’t assume that a translation captures every nuance; use a good Catholic translation, with notes. Ask questions; it’s fine to say, ‘I don’t understand this.’ And pray before you read: ‘Come, Holy Spirit.’ The same Spirit who inspired the text helps us to understand it.”
ask: What are the three guidelines from Dei Verbum? (Unity of Scripture, living Tradition, analogy of faith.)
What are the four questions? (What does it say, mean, point to, ask of me?)
What should we do before reading? (Pray to the Holy Spirit.)
practice: Choose a short Gospel passage, such as Mark 10:46-52 (Bartimaeus).
On a sheet with four boxes, answer the four questions.
Check the footnotes in a Catholic Bible for the Old Testament connection.
Share what the passage asks of you.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, open our minds to your word.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use the four questions on the next Sunday Gospel.”

tryit: Use the four questions on a Gospel passage.
Write your answers.
Say what the passage asks of you.
lessons.saintStory:
Bede was born around 673 in northern England and was given at seven to the monastery at Wearmouth, and later lived at Jarrow. He spent his whole life there in prayer, study, teaching and writing. He wrote on Scripture, on science and on history. His Ecclesiastical History of the English People is the main source for early English history.
Bede loved the Gospels and wrote commentaries on them. In 735, when he was sick and near death, he was working on a translation of the Gospel of John into English, so that those who could not read Latin could hear it. His pupil Cuthbert wrote that Bede kept dictating through the day, and told his scribe to write quickly. As evening came, the scribe said, “There is still one sentence left.” Bede said, “Write it quickly.” When it was done, he said, “It is finished,” and died.
Bede is a Doctor of the Church.

lessons.title: The Word became flesh
lessons.idea: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Jesus is true God and true man: one divine Person with two natures, fully divine and fully human. John’s prologue states it beautifully.
lessons.question: What does the Incarnation show?
lessons.activity: “Prologue in pieces” (30 min). Read John 1:1–18 in parts. Students highlight key words (Word, with God, was God, flesh, light, grace and truth). Then explain the prologue in a 60-second talk to a partner, using the terms person and nature.
teach: The Word (Logos) was in the beginning, with God and was God, and became flesh (John 1:1, 14; CCC 461–463). He did not cease to be God.
The Council of Chalcedon (451) taught: one Person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation (CCC 464–469). Jesus has a human body, soul, mind and will.
Heresies to name: Arianism (Jesus is a creature), Docetism (he only seemed human), Nestorianism (two persons), Monophysitism (one nature). Each was condemned (CCC 465–467).
The Incarnation is the source of the sacraments: God uses material things because God became matter.
talk: What does the Incarnation show about matter and the body?
Which heresy denies his humanity? His divinity?
quiz: The Incarnation is…|A parable|A metaphor|God becoming man|Man becoming God|2|CCC 461.
Docetism denied…|His birth|His death|Christ’s real humanity|His divinity|2|CCC 465.
Chalcedon taught…|One nature|Two natures in one Person|No Person|Two Persons|1|CCC 467.
lessons.life: Pray John 1:1–14 slowly.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: the bishop who stood against the world to defend that Jesus is truly God.
misc: “Jesus was God pretending to be man.”
lessons.mem: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14)
lessons.hook: Ask, “If you wanted to show someone who you are, what is the best way?” Show a picture and then show yourself. God did the second: he came himself in Jesus.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “one Person, two natures” and name one heresy it rules out.

script.open: Write on the board, ‘God became a baby.’ Say, “Say that out loud and listen to how strange it sounds. Why would God do it?” Collect reactions before moving to John 1.
teach: Read John 1:1-14. Say: “‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.’ This is the Incarnation: God the Son took on a human nature. The word comes from the Latin carnis, ‘flesh.’ Jesus is not half God and half man, nor a god disguised as a man, nor a man who became God. He is one Person, the eternal Son of God, who is fully God and fully man.”

Say: “The Church defined this over the first centuries. Nicaea in 325: Jesus is God, ‘consubstantial’ with the Father. Ephesus in 431: Mary is Theotokos, ‘God-bearer,’ because the Person she bore is God. Chalcedon in 451: Jesus has two natures, divine and human, united in one Person ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.’ This means that Jesus has a human body, mind and will, and he is also God. He felt hunger, tears and fear. He also forgave sins, calmed storms and raised the dead.”

Say: “Why did God become man? The Catechism gives four reasons: to save us by reconciling us with God; to show us God’s love; to be our model of holiness; and to make us sharers in the divine nature. Only a man could die for our sins, and only God could save. St. Athanasius said, ‘The Son of God became man so that we might become God.’ He did not mean that we become gods, but share in God’s life by grace. The mystery of Christmas is that God has come among us, in the flesh.”
ask: What is the Incarnation? (God the Son took on a human nature.)
How many natures does Jesus have, and how many Persons? (Two natures, one Person.)
Why did the Son of God become man? (To save us, show God’s love, be our model, and share God’s life with us.)
practice: Draw a chart with two columns: “Jesus shows his divinity” and “Jesus shows his humanity.”
Search the Gospels for examples: Mark 4:35-41 (asleep, then stills the storm); John 11 (weeps, then raises Lazarus); Mark 2:1-12 (forgives sins); John 4:6 (tired).
Add three of your own.
Write one sentence: why both natures are necessary.
script.close: Pray the Nicene Creed lines, “For us men and for our salvation…” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Bow your head at the words ‘and became man’ at Mass.”

tryit: Fill in the two natures chart.
Mark what Scripture shows of each.
Explain why both are needed.
lessons.saintStory:
Athanasius was born around 296 in Alexandria, Egypt. As a young deacon, he went with his bishop to the Council of Nicaea in 325, to answer a priest named Arius, who taught that the Son of God was a creature, made by the Father. The Council declared that the Son is “of one substance with the Father.”
The fight was not over. Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria in 328. For decades, emperors favored Arius’s followers. Athanasius was exiled five times, over seventeen years, in the desert and in Rome and Gaul. He kept writing and teaching. In his book On the Incarnation, he explained that God became man so that humans could share in his life: “He became man that we might become God.”
He died in 373. A saying about him was “Athanasius against the world.” His faith is in the Creed we say each Sunday.

lessons.title: Annunciation and birth
lessons.idea: Luke and Matthew tell the infancy of Jesus from different perspectives: Luke from Mary’s viewpoint with angels and shepherds, Matthew from Joseph’s with the magi. Together they reveal Jesus as Son of God, Son of David and Savior of all nations.
lessons.question: What do we learn from the infancy accounts?
lessons.activity: “Two infancy narratives” (30 min). Students compare Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2 in a two-column chart: who receives the message, who visits, what Old Testament texts are cited, what is the mood. Identify shared facts: Bethlehem, virgin birth, Joseph of David’s line, Nazareth.
teach: The infancy narratives reveal Jesus’ identity (CCC 496–507, 525–530). Luke has the Annunciation, Visitation, the shepherds, Simeon and Anna; Matthew has the dream of Joseph, the magi, Herod and the flight to Egypt.
Mary’s Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) sings of a God who lifts the lowly. The magi show that Gentiles come to worship (Epiphany; CCC 528).
The virginal conception is taught in both Gospels (CCC 496–498). Jesus is born in Bethlehem, the city of David (Micah 5:2).
Differences in detail are not contradictions but complementary views. Avoid forcing a mixed account.
talk: What do the narratives say about who Jesus is?
quiz: Mary conceived by…|An angel|A prophet|Joseph|The Holy Spirit|3|Luke 1:35.
Jesus was born in…|Nazareth|Cana|Bethlehem|Rome|2|Luke 2:4-7.
Matthew emphasizes…|The shepherds|Mary’s Magnificat|The census only|Fulfilment of prophecy|3|Matthew 1-2.
lessons.life: Read Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2 in a week.
lessons.saint: Joseph, husband of Mary: a righteous man who listened to angels in dreams.
misc: “The Christmas story is a fairy tale.”
“Three kings arrived at the manger on December 25.”
lessons.mem: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.” (Luke 1:46–47)
lessons.hook: Say: “Imagine telling the story of a birth from the mother’s viewpoint, then from the father’s.” That is what Luke and Matthew do.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three details unique to Luke, three unique to Matthew and one shared by both.

script.open: Read aloud Luke 1:26-38 without comment, then ask the students to close their eyes and picture Mary’s face when she hears the angel. Ask them to describe what they saw.
teach: Read Luke 1:26-38. Say: “The angel Gabriel was sent to a virgin in Nazareth named Mary. ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.’ She was troubled. The angel told her she would conceive and bear a son named Jesus, who would be great and reign on David’s throne forever. She asked, ‘How can this be, since I have no husband?’ The angel said the Holy Spirit would overshadow her. ‘For nothing will be impossible with God.’ Mary said, ‘Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.’ The Word became flesh at that moment. We remember it at the Angelus.”

Say: “The Church teaches that Mary was a virgin when she conceived Jesus, by the power of the Holy Spirit, with no human father. This is the Virginal Conception. It shows that Jesus’ conception was God’s initiative, a new creation. She remained a virgin ever after. And ‘full of grace’ points to the Immaculate Conception: Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her existence, to be a fitting mother for the Son of God. Mary’s ‘yes’ was free. God asked, and waited.”

Read Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 2:1-20 in summary. Say: “Joseph, told in a dream, took Mary as his wife. Because of a census by Caesar Augustus, they traveled to Bethlehem, David’s town. There was no room at the inn, so Jesus was born and laid in a manger. Angels appeared to shepherds: ‘Fear not; for behold, I bring you good news of a great joy… to you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.’ The shepherds, humble people, were the first to be told. Later the magi came from the East, following a star, and brought gold, frankincense and myrrh. Herod tried to kill the child, and the family fled to Egypt. Matthew sees in this the new Moses and Israel.”
ask: What did Mary say to the angel? (Let it be to me according to your word.)
What did the angel tell Joseph to do? (Take Mary as his wife and name the child Jesus.)
Who were the first to hear the news of Jesus’ birth? (Shepherds.)
practice: Make two columns: “The angel asks” and “The answer.”
Fill in for Mary (Luke 1) and Joseph (Matthew 1).
Add a row for the shepherds and a row for the magi.
Write one thing you learn from their response about how to respond to God.
script.close: Pray the Angelus or the Hail Mary. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Angelus with your family.”

tryit: Read Luke 1:26-38 and Matthew 1:18-25.
Mark what the angel asked of each.
Write each answer.
lessons.saintStory:
Joseph was a descendant of David, living in Nazareth, who worked as a carpenter and was engaged to Mary. When he learned she was with child, he was troubled. Matthew says that being a righteous man and unwilling to put her to shame, he resolved to divorce her quietly.
But an angel appeared to him in a dream, and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit; she will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” Joseph woke and did as the angel commanded.
The Gospels never record a word spoken by Joseph. Yet at every turn he acts: taking Mary home, going to Bethlehem for the census, fleeing to Egypt and returning to Nazareth. Each time, he obeys a dream. He is patron of the universal Church.

lessons.title: The hidden life
lessons.idea: For about thirty years Jesus lived in Nazareth, obeying Mary and Joseph, learning a trade and praying. This “hidden life” makes ordinary life holy. Luke gives us one glimpse at twelve, when Jesus stays in the Temple.
lessons.question: Why was it hidden?
lessons.activity: “A day in Nazareth” (30 min). Using historical background (village life, carpentry, synagogue school, family prayer), students write a short diary entry for a day in the Holy Family’s home. Include prayer and work. Read Luke 2:41–52.
teach: The hidden life (CCC 531–534): Jesus obeyed, worked and prayed. He sanctified family life and work (CCC 532).
Joseph, the just man, guarded and provided (Matthew 1:19). Mary kept all these things in her heart (Luke 2:51). Jesus was “subject to them” (CCC 532).
At twelve he said, “I must be in my Father’s house” (Luke 2:49): the first words of Jesus in the Gospel show his divine mission.
Link to Catholic teaching on the dignity of work and the importance of family prayer.
talk: How does it sanctify our daily life?
How do you honor your parents?
quiz: Jesus lived in Nazareth for about…|Thirty years|One year|Three years|Ten years|0|CCC 534.
At twelve he was found in…|Capernaum|Egypt|Cana|The Temple|3|Luke 2:46.
He was subject to…|The king|The priests|No one|Mary and Joseph|3|Luke 2:51.
lessons.life: Offer your ordinary tasks to God.
lessons.saint: Thérèse of Lisieux: a young nun who made ordinary things great by love.
lessons.mem: “And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and man.” (Luke 2:52)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do we know about Jesus’ first thirty years?” (almost nothing). “Why would God spend most of his time on earth in ordinary life?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain why the hidden life matters for ordinary people.

script.open: Ask, “What did Jesus do for thirty years before he began teaching? How much of his life was ‘ordinary’?” Write on the board: 30 years hidden, 3 years public.
teach: Read Luke 2:39-40 and 2:51-52. Say: “‘The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the favor of God was upon him.’ ‘He went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them… And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and man.’ The Gospels say very little about Jesus’ first thirty years. He lived in Nazareth, in a small village, in a carpenter’s house. He learned a trade, learned the Scriptures, and prayed the psalms with his family. He was obedient to Mary and Joseph.”

Read Luke 2:41-52. Say: “The only story of Jesus’ childhood is when he was twelve. His family went to Jerusalem for Passover, and he stayed behind in the Temple. After three days, they found him among the teachers. ‘Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?’ This is the first hint of his identity. Notice that then he went back with them and obeyed. Mary kept all these things in her heart.”

Say: “Why does it matter? First, it shows the dignity of ordinary life: family, work and obedience. By living thirty years in a hidden way, Jesus made ordinary life holy. Second, it shows the importance of the family. The Holy Family is a model. Pope Leo XIII said that in the Holy Family, all domestic virtues shine. Third, it shows that God can be found in the ordinary. We do not need to do something spectacular to be holy. Doing our work well and with love, as Thérèse did, is holiness.”
ask: How long was Jesus’ hidden life? (About thirty years.)
What did he say at twelve in the Temple? (I must be in my Father’s house.)
Why does the hidden life matter? (It makes ordinary life holy and shows the value of family and work.)
practice: Draw a clock of your day from morning to night.
Mark the ordinary tasks: waking up, dishes, homework, walking, waiting.
Beside three of them write a short offering, such as “For you, Jesus.”
Choose one to do especially well today.
script.close: Pray the Morning Offering. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do the dishes or a chore with love, for Jesus.”

tryit: List the small things in your own day.
Offer each one with love.
Choose one to do for Jesus today.
lessons.saintStory:
Thérèse Martin was born in 1873 in Alençon, France. Her mother died when she was four, and her family moved to Lisieux. At fifteen she asked permission to enter the Carmelite convent, and when the bishop said no, she asked the pope himself, kneeling in Rome. At fifteen and a half she was admitted.
In the convent she did ordinary things: washing, sewing, sweeping, kitchen work, being polite to a sister who annoyed her. She saw that she could not do great things like the missionaries and martyrs she admired. But she found what she called her “little way”: to do small things with great love. “Love proves itself by deeds,” she wrote.
She died of tuberculosis at twenty-four, in 1897. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, made her famous around the world. She is a Doctor of the Church and patron of missions. She shows what Jesus’ thirty hidden years can teach us.

units.title: The public ministry
units.eq: What did Jesus teach and do?

lessons.title: Baptism and temptation
lessons.idea: At the Jordan, Jesus is baptized, the heavens open, and the Father and the Spirit identify him as the beloved Son. In the desert he faces the same temptations that Israel and Adam failed, and he overcomes them.
lessons.question: What does the baptism of Jesus show?
lessons.activity: “Three temptations” (30 min). Match each temptation (stones to bread, jump from the Temple, kingdoms of the world) with an Israel failure in the desert (manna, testing God, idolatry) and with a modern parallel (comfort, showing off, power). Note which scripture Jesus quotes each time (Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13).
teach: The baptism of Jesus reveals the Trinity: the Father’s voice, the Spirit as a dove, the Son (CCC 535–537). It anticipates our own Baptism and his Passion.
The temptation in the desert recalls Israel’s forty years and Adam’s fall (CCC 538–540). Jesus resists with the Word of God.
He is the new Adam and the new Israel. Lent follows these forty days (CCC 540).
Temptation is not sin. Jesus “has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
talk: How do the temptations parallel Israel?
quiz: At the baptism the Spirit descended as…|A star|A flame|A cloud|A dove|3|Matthew 3:16.
Jesus fasted…|Seven days|Three days|Ten days|Forty days|3|Matthew 4:2.
He answered temptation with…|Anger|Scripture|Silence|Magic|1|Matthew 4:4.
lessons.life: Memorize one Scripture to use against temptation.
lessons.saint: Antony of the Desert: a young man who went into the wilderness to fight temptation and found God.
misc: “Jesus needed to be baptized for his sins.”
lessons.mem: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.” (Matthew 4:4)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Why would a sinless man need baptism?” Then listen to Matthew 3:13–17. Jesus joins us; he shares our life so that he can lift it.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain what the baptism and temptation reveal about Jesus.

script.open: Show a map of the Jordan River and the Judean desert. Say, “Jesus goes from the river to the wilderness in a single chapter. Why would a place so empty be the next stop after Baptism?” Take guesses.
teach: Read Matthew 3:13-17. Say: “Jesus came from Nazareth to the Jordan to be baptized by John. John protested: ‘I need to be baptized by you.’ Jesus said, ‘Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’ He had no sin, but he went into the water to join sinners, and to show where he was going. As he came up, the heavens opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and a voice said, ‘This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.’ All three Persons of the Trinity are present.”

Read Matthew 4:1-11. Say: “Right after this, the Spirit led Jesus into the desert, where he fasted forty days. The devil tempted him three times. First, ‘If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.’ Jesus answered, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’ Second, the devil took him to the top of the Temple: ‘Throw yourself down.’ Jesus said, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’ Third, he showed him all the kingdoms: ‘All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.’ Jesus said, ‘Begone, Satan! You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’”

Say: “Notice that each temptation offered a shortcut: comfort, a showy sign, power. Israel failed similar tests in the desert for forty years. Adam failed in the garden. Jesus succeeded as the new Israel and the new Adam. He answered each time with Scripture, from Deuteronomy. Jesus knows what temptation is like (Hebrews 4:15). We too will be tempted. We fight with prayer, fasting, Scripture and the sacraments. Lent, forty days, follows Jesus into the desert.”
ask: Who was present at Jesus’ baptism? (The Father, Son and Holy Spirit.)
How did Jesus answer the devil? (With Scripture.)
How are we helped against temptation? (Prayer, fasting, Scripture, sacraments.)
practice: Make a three-row chart for the temptations: what the devil offered, what Jesus answered, a modern version.
For the modern versions, think of comfort (give in to what I want now), showing off (look important), and power (take a shortcut).
Write the Scripture answer for each.
Pick one scripture line to memorize.
script.close: Pray: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose a small fast for the week.”

tryit: Compare Adam’s test and Jesus’ test.
Write each temptation and the answer.
Find a modern version.
lessons.saintStory:
Antony was born in Egypt around 251 to a wealthy Christian family. When he was about twenty, his parents died. At Mass he heard the Gospel, “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” He took it as meant for him. He gave away his land, sold his goods and went to live as a hermit.
He lived in a tomb, then in the desert, in an abandoned fort. He fought fierce temptations, which his friend Athanasius, who wrote his life, described as demons appearing in many forms. He prayed, fasted, worked and read Scripture. People came to him for advice and prayers, and he taught them. Many moved to the desert to live as he did, and he is called the father of monks.
He lived to be 105, and died in 356. He said, “Whoever hammers a lump of iron first decides what he is going to make of it.”

lessons.title: The Kingdom and parables
lessons.idea: Jesus proclaimed the Kingdom of God, which has come near in his person. He taught in parables, short stories from daily life that reveal and conceal, inviting listeners to decide.
lessons.question: Why parables?
lessons.activity: “Interpret three parables” (30 min). Groups take one parable each: sower (Mark 4:1–20), mustard seed and leaven (Matthew 13:31–33), lost sheep or prodigal son (Luke 15). Students retell it, name the surprise, and state what it says about the Kingdom and about us.
teach: The Kingdom of God is the reign of God in Christ, already present and still to come (CCC 541–546, 2816). Jesus invites all to enter, especially the poor and sinners.
Parables use ordinary images (seeds, coins, sheep) to reveal what God is like. They also call for a response: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark 4:9; Matthew 13:10–17).
Key parables: sower, weeds, mustard seed, leaven, treasure, pearl, net, lost sheep, lost coin, prodigal son, good Samaritan.
Resist reducing parables to morals; look for the shock of grace.
quiz: The Kingdom of God is…|A territory|God’s reign begun in Christ|A party|A building|1|CCC 541.
The parable of the sower shows…|Politics|Economics|Farming tips|Different responses to the word|3|Mark 4.
Jesus told parables to…|Reveal truths to those open|Hide from soldiers|Make money|Confuse everyone|0|Matthew 13.
lessons.life: Read a parable each day for a week.
lessons.saint: Monica: a mother who sowed prayer and tears for seventeen years.
misc: “The Kingdom of God is only heaven after death.”
lessons.mem: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field.” (Matthew 13:31)
lessons.hook: Tell a short parable of your own (e.g., a lost phone found with great joy). Ask what it means. “Jesus told stories like this to make people think.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell a parable and explain what it reveals about God’s Kingdom.

script.open: Hold up a mustard seed or a poppy seed in a clear dish. Pass it around. Say, “Something this small became the picture Jesus used for the Kingdom. What would you have picked?” Take suggestions.
teach: Read Mark 1:14-15. Say: “‘The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent, and believe in the gospel.’ The Kingdom of God, or of heaven, was the center of Jesus’ preaching. It is God’s reign, his rule of love and justice, which is present now in Jesus, grows in the Church, and will be complete at the end of time. It is a gift, and we must accept it with repentance and faith. The Church is its seed and beginning.”

Say: “Jesus taught about the Kingdom in parables, which are short stories from daily life that have a deeper meaning. The sower (Mark 4): the seed is the word, and the soils are the ways we receive it: path, rocky ground, thorns, good soil. The mustard seed: the Kingdom starts tiny and grows large. The leaven: it works quietly through all the dough. The treasure and the pearl: it is worth everything. The lost sheep, lost coin and prodigal son (Luke 15): God rejoices over sinners who return. The good Samaritan (Luke 10): who is my neighbor? Anyone in need. The talents (Matthew 25): use what God gave you.”

Say: “Why parables? They invite listening. Some heard and understood; some did not. Jesus often explained them privately to the disciples. Each parable has a main point, and we shouldn’t make every detail an allegory. The parables ask for a response. Read the parable of the Prodigal Son and ask: Which character am I? The father who forgives? The younger son who left? The older brother who resents? Each reveals something of the Father’s mercy.”
ask: What is the Kingdom of God? (God’s reign, present in Jesus and growing in the Church.)
What does the parable of the mustard seed teach? (The Kingdom begins small and grows great.)
Why did Jesus teach in parables? (To invite listening and lead to a deeper meaning.)
practice: Make a card for each parable: sower, mustard seed, leaven, treasure, pearl, lost sheep, prodigal son, good Samaritan.
Match each to a meaning card.
Choose one parable and draw it on a sheet.
Under the picture, write what it says about the Kingdom and one thing it asks of you.
script.close: Pray: “Thy kingdom come.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read the parable of the prodigal son and ask which character you are.”

tryit: Match each parable to its meaning.
Draw the sower, the mustard seed or the lost sheep.
Write one line on what it says about the Kingdom.
lessons.saintStory:
Monica was born in North Africa in 331. She was a Christian, and married a man named Patricius, who was not and who had a hot temper. She was patient with him, and he became a Christian shortly before he died. Her eldest son Augustine, a brilliant young man, was a different story. He left the faith, lived a wild life, and joined a sect.
Monica prayed for him and wept. A bishop who consoled her said, “It is not possible that the son of so many tears should perish.” When Augustine went to Italy, she followed him, to Milan. There he met Ambrose, and began to question his life. After seventeen years of her prayers, Augustine was baptized in 387.
Monica died soon afterward, at Ostia, on the way back to Africa. Her last words to Augustine were that nothing was far from God, and to remember her at the altar. Her patience was like the seed that grows slowly.

lessons.title: Miracles as signs
lessons.idea: Jesus’ miracles are signs of the Kingdom. They show his power over nature, sickness, demons and death, they accompany his word, and they call for faith. They are not magic or show.
lessons.question: What do miracles signify?
lessons.activity: “Classify the signs” (30 min). Sort miracles into categories: nature (calming the storm), healing (blind man), exorcism (Gerasene demoniac), raising the dead (Lazarus). For each, name what it reveals about Jesus and what response it asks.
teach: Miracles accompany his words and show the Kingdom’s arrival (CCC 547–550). Jesus does not remove all evil, but frees people from it as a sign of his saving mission.
They call for faith: “Your faith has made you well” (Mark 5:34). Jesus refuses to work signs to satisfy curiosity (Matthew 12:38–39).
John calls them “signs” and uses them to lead to deeper truths: the bread of life, the light of the world, the resurrection and the life.
Cana (John 2) also shows Mary’s intercession and the transformation of marriage (CCC 1613).
talk: Why does Jesus often ask for faith?
quiz: Miracles are…|Signs of the Kingdom|Tricks|Legends|Natural events|0|CCC 547.
The first sign in John is…|Raising Lazarus|Feeding|Cana|Walking on water|2|John 2:11.
Jesus often asks for…|Silence|Faith|Money|Fasting|1|Mark 5:34.
lessons.life: List the miracles of Mark 1–5.
lessons.saint: Bernadette Soubirous: a poor girl at Lourdes, through whom a spring of healing water flowed.
lessons.mem: “Do whatever he tells you.” (John 2:5)
lessons.hook: Read John 2:1–11. Ask: “Why did John call the water into wine a ‘sign’?” Signs point beyond themselves.
lessons.assess: Ask students to choose one miracle, say what it reveals about Jesus and what response it asks.

script.open: Ask, “Do you think miracles still happen? Why would God do a miracle? What is it for?” Take a few answers.
teach: Say: “The Gospels record about thirty-five miracles of Jesus. They are of four kinds. Healings: the blind man, the lepers, the paralytic, the woman with the flow of blood. Nature miracles: the calming of the storm, walking on water, the feeding of the five thousand. Exorcisms: casting out demons. Raising the dead: Jairus’s daughter, the widow’s son at Nain, Lazarus. The Gospel of John calls them ‘signs.’ A sign points to something beyond itself.”

Say: “What do the miracles show? They show who Jesus is: he has power over sickness, nature, evil and death, which only God has. They show the Kingdom breaking in: Jesus said, ‘If it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.’ (Luke 11:20) They show his compassion: he was ‘moved with pity.’ And they call for faith. Often Jesus said, ‘Your faith has made you well.’ Jesus refused to work miracles to show off.”

Read John 6:1-15 and 20:30-31 in summary. Say: “When Jesus fed five thousand, the crowd wanted to make him king. But the next day, he told them that he is the bread of life. The sign pointed to the Eucharist. John says, ‘These are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ.’ Miracles continue in the Church, in saints, in healings at Lourdes, and above all in the sacraments. The Church investigates carefully, and only after rigorous study declares a healing inexplicable. The greatest miracles are the ones inside: forgiveness and conversion.”
ask: Name four kinds of miracles in the Gospels. (Healings, nature, exorcisms, raising the dead.)
What do miracles show? (Who Jesus is, that the Kingdom has come, his compassion.)
What did the feeding of the five thousand point to? (The Eucharist.)
practice: Prepare a list of miracles with references: Mark 2:1-12, Mark 4:35-41, Mark 5:1-20, Luke 7:11-17, John 2:1-11, John 6:1-15, John 11.
Groups sort them into the four types.
For each, write what it reveals about Jesus.
Pick one and write what it asks of us.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.” (Mark 9:24.) Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for a sick person you know.”

tryit: Classify the miracle stories.
Say what each sign reveals.
Read John 20:30-31.
lessons.saintStory:
Bernadette Soubirous was born in 1844 in Lourdes, in the south of France. Her family had been millers and fell into poverty, and by 1858 they were living in a one-room former jail cell. She was fourteen, small and sickly, with asthma, and had not been to school.
On February 11, 1858, she went to gather firewood by the river, and saw in a grotto a lady in white with a blue sash and a rosary. She went back eighteen times. The lady asked for prayer and penance, and told her, “I am the Immaculate Conception.” She also told her to dig in the ground, where a spring began to flow. The authorities questioned her harshly, but she remained calm and truthful.
Bernadette became a sister at Nevers, where she nursed the sick, and she died at thirty-five in 1879. Lourdes is now a place of pilgrimage, where many sick people come to pray, and the Church has recognized many healings as miraculous.

units.title: The Sermon on the Mount
units.eq: How does Jesus teach us to live?

lessons.title: The Beatitudes
lessons.idea: The Beatitudes are Jesus’ portrait of the way to true happiness. They begin the Sermon on the Mount, are promises as much as challenges, and describe Jesus himself.
lessons.question: Why “blessed”?
lessons.activity: “Beatitudes memory and reflection” (30 min). Students memorize the eight, then pair each with a saint or contemporary example and with one practical choice. Silent reflection: which Beatitude challenges me most?
teach: The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12; Luke 6:20–26) are the heart of Jesus’ preaching (CCC 1716). They fulfill the promises made to Abraham and point to the Kingdom.
They describe the vocation of the faithful: share Christ’s Passion and Resurrection (CCC 1717). Each blessing has a reward now and later.
“Poor in spirit” means depending on God. “Pure in heart” means undivided love. “Meek” is strength under control.
They answer the desire for happiness that God has placed in every heart (CCC 1718–1719).
talk: How do they differ from culture?
quiz: The Beatitudes are the path to…|Power|Fame|Wealth|Happiness|3|CCC 1720.
Blessed are the pure in heart for they shall…|See God|Be satisfied|Be comforted|Inherit land|0|Matthew 5:8.
Beatitude means…|Rest|Law|Fear|Blessedness|3|CCC 1716.
lessons.life: Memorize the Beatitudes.
lessons.saint: Josephine Bakhita: a former slave who forgave and was called ‘lucky’.
misc: “Being poor in spirit means low self-esteem.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” (Matthew 5:3)
lessons.hook: Poll the class: “What do people say make you happy?” Then read Matthew 5:3–12 and ask which are surprising.
lessons.assess: Ask students to recite the eight Beatitudes and explain one in their own words.

script.open: Write on the board, ‘Blessed are…’ and give each student a minute to complete the sentence with a person the world calls successful. Then read the Beatitudes and compare. Say, “Whose list is different from the world’s?”
teach: Read Matthew 5:1-12. Say: “Jesus went up on the mountain, sat down like a teacher, and spoke to his disciples. The word ‘Beatitude’ comes from the Latin for blessed, or happy. Each begins, ‘Blessed are…’ They are the heart of the Sermon on the Mount. They describe what the Kingdom looks like and the path to true happiness. They surprise us: blessed are the poor, the mourning, the meek, the persecuted. Jesus turns our idea of success upside down.”

Say: “Here are the eight. The poor in spirit: those who depend on God, not on themselves. Those who mourn: who grieve for sin and loss; God comforts. The meek: gentle, not harsh; they will inherit the earth. Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: who want justice and holiness. The merciful: who forgive and help; they receive mercy. The pure in heart: single-hearted, who will see God. The peacemakers: who work for reconciliation; they will be called children of God. Those persecuted for righteousness’ sake: who suffer for doing good; theirs is the Kingdom. The first and last have the same reward: the Kingdom of heaven.”

Say: “The Beatitudes are a portrait of Christ himself, who was poor, meek, merciful and persecuted. They answer our deepest desire for happiness, which is a desire for God. The Catechism says they teach us the final end to which God calls us: the Kingdom, the vision of God, entering into the joy of the Lord. They are not just ideals for a few, but a path for all disciples. The saints lived them.”
ask: What does ‘blessed’ mean? (Happy; truly fulfilled in God.)
What is the reward of the poor in spirit? (The Kingdom of heaven.)
Who is the Beatitudes’ perfect portrait? (Jesus.)
practice: Write the eight Beatitudes on a sheet. Beside each, rewrite it in your own words.
Think of a person (a saint, a family member or a public figure) who lives each.
Choose one Beatitude to practice, and write one specific action.
Share it with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Beatitudes slowly, one student reading, all responding, “Blessed are you.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Practice one Beatitude all week.”

tryit: Rewrite each Beatitude in your own words.
Find a saint or a person for each.
Choose one to live this week.
lessons.saintStory:
Bakhita was born around 1869 in Darfur, in Sudan. When she was about seven, slave traders kidnapped her. The shock was so great that she forgot her own name, and the traders called her Bakhita, which means “lucky.” She was sold several times, and one owner had her whipped and cut so badly that she bore scars for life.
She was bought by an Italian consul, who treated her kindly, and brought her to Italy. She was given to a family as a nanny, and she went with the child to a school run by the Canossian Sisters in Venice. There she learned about God. She had always known that someone made the world; now she knew his name. She was baptized in 1890, and refused to return to Sudan, because she was now free under Italian law. She became a sister in 1893.
She served for fifty years, as cook, sacristan and porter, and was loved for her gentleness. She said that if she met her kidnappers, she would kneel and kiss their hands, because without them she would not be a Christian. She died in 1947 and was named a saint in 2000.

lessons.title: Fulfilling the Law
lessons.idea: Jesus did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it, going to the heart: not only “do not kill” but do not hate; not only “do not commit adultery” but do not lust. “You have heard… but I say to you.”
lessons.question: What does “you have heard…” mean?
lessons.activity: “Antitheses” (30 min). Students fill a chart with six antitheses from Matthew 5 (anger, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, enemies): the old rule, Jesus’ deepening, and a modern application. Discuss why the demand is high and what gives us the strength (grace).
teach: Jesus “fulfills” the Law (Matthew 5:17; CCC 577–582). He is the only one who kept it perfectly and he gives its inner meaning.
The New Law is a law of love and grace (CCC 1965–1974). The Sermon on the Mount gives its charter. “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).
The Church distinguishes moral, ceremonial and judicial precepts (CCC 1961–1964). The moral law remains; ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ.
Interpret hard sayings (e.g., plucking out an eye) as strong ways of urging seriousness about sin.
talk: What is different in Jesus’s teaching?
quiz: Jesus came to…|Ignore it|Abolish the Law|Amend it slightly|Fulfill the Law|3|Matthew 5:17.
“Love your enemies” is…|Part of the Sermon on the Mount|From Proverbs|Optional|From Exodus|0|Matthew 5:44.
The new law is written…|In books only|In the air|On hearts|On stone|2|CCC 1966.
lessons.life: Pray for someone who has hurt you.
lessons.saint: Stephen: the first martyr, who forgave those who stoned him.
lessons.mem: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.” (Matthew 5:17)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Is it enough to avoid hitting someone? What about words?” Read Matthew 5:21–22.
lessons.assess: Ask students to restate two antitheses and explain how Jesus deepens the law.

script.open: Present two rules side by side: ‘Do not hit.’ and ‘Do not even be angry.’ Ask, “Which is easier to keep? Which one changes a person?” Take answers and use them to read Matthew 5:21-22.
teach: Read Matthew 5:17-20. Say: “‘Think not that I have come to abolish the law and the prophets; I have come not to abolish them but to fulfill them.’ Jesus is not against the Law of Moses. He completes it, and shows what it was always meant to be. In the rest of the chapter, he gives six examples, each beginning, ‘You have heard that it was said… But I say to you.’ He goes to the heart.”

Say: “You have heard ‘You shall not kill’; but I say, do not even be angry with your brother, and make peace quickly. You have heard ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say, anyone who looks with lust has already sinned in his heart. You have heard ‘an eye for an eye’; but I say, do not resist an evil person, turn the other cheek, go the extra mile. You have heard ‘love your neighbor and hate your enemy’; but I say, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good. And finally: ‘You, therefore, must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.’”

Say: “Notice what Jesus does. He moves from external actions to inner attitudes: anger, lust, desire for revenge. He raises the bar. This is impossible by our own strength; it is possible by grace. Stephen did it when he prayed for his killers. Jesus did it on the cross. This is the New Law, the law of love. It is lived with the help of the Holy Spirit, who is poured into our hearts. Where the Old Law said ‘Do not,’ the New says ‘Love.’”
ask: Did Jesus abolish the Law? (No, he fulfilled it.)
What does Jesus say about anger? (It is where killing begins; make peace quickly.)
How did Stephen live the New Law? (He forgave his killers.)
practice: Make a three-column chart: “You have heard,” “But I say,” “In my life.”
Fill in three of the Sermon on the Mount pairs from Matthew 5:21-48.
In the third column, write a specific example of how to live it.
Pick one and carry it out this week.
script.close: Pray Stephen’s prayer: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for someone who is hard to love.”

tryit: List the ‘You have heard… but I say’ pairs.
Say what Jesus adds to each.
Write one for your own life.
lessons.saintStory:
Stephen was one of the first seven deacons, chosen by the apostles to serve the poor widows in the Jerusalem community. He was “full of faith and of the Holy Spirit,” and worked wonders among the people. Some men argued with him and could not withstand his wisdom, so they made false charges that he spoke against Moses and the Temple.
Stephen was brought before the council, and gave a long speech, recalling how God had called Israel, and how the people had resisted the prophets. “You always resist the Holy Spirit.” They were furious. Stephen looked up and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God.” They dragged him out of the city and stoned him. A young man named Saul held the coats.
As he died, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And, kneeling, he cried, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Saul, who watched, became the apostle Paul.

lessons.title: Prayer, almsgiving, fasting
lessons.idea: Jesus teaches three practices of devotion: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. He warns us to do them for God, not for show. The Our Father sits at the center. These practices are the traditional works of Lent.
lessons.question: Why in secret?
lessons.activity: “Lenten plan” (30 min). Students plan a realistic Lent with one practice in each category: prayer (daily time), fasting (from a food, media or a habit), almsgiving (money or time for others). They discuss how to keep it hidden. Read Matthew 6:1–18.
teach: Almsgiving, prayer and fasting are ways to turn back to God (CCC 1434–1438). They are the Church’s penitential practices.
Jesus insists on secrecy of heart: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:4). Hypocrisy empties religion.
He gives the Our Father as the model of prayer (Matthew 6:9–13; CCC 2759–2776). Fasting trains us to hunger for God.
Church law: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fast and abstinence; Fridays of Lent are days of abstinence (CCC 2043).
quiz: Jesus teaches to pray…|Never|On street corners|Loudly|In secret|3|Matthew 6:6.
The three works are…|Read, write, speak|Faith, hope, love|Prayer, fasting, almsgiving|Work, rest, play|2|Matthew 6.
The Our Father is found in…|Acts 2|John 3|Matthew 6|Mark 1|2|Matthew 6:9.
lessons.life: Plan a concrete Lenten practice.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth of Hungary: a young queen who fed the hungry and nursed lepers.
misc: “Giving up chocolate for Lent is enough.”
lessons.mem: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” (Matthew 6:6)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Would you rather be applauded or be quietly true?” Read Matthew 6:1–4.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the three practices and why Jesus says to do them in secret.

script.open: Ask, “Is it wrong to want people to know you did a good thing? Why would Jesus tell us to do some good things in secret?”
teach: Read Matthew 6:1-18 in sections. Say: “Jesus names three traditional works of piety: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. Each time he says, ‘When you give alms… when you pray… when you fast…’ — not ‘if.’ And each time, he warns about doing it to be seen by others. ‘Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.’ ‘Go into your room and shut the door.’ ‘Anoint your head and wash your face.’ The Father who sees in secret will reward you.”

Say: “Almsgiving is giving to the poor out of love. Not leftovers, but sacrifice. It is a work of mercy and justice, and it frees us from loving money too much. Prayer is conversation with God; Jesus then gives the Our Father. Fasting is going without food or something good in order to grow in self-control and to show that we depend on God. The Church asks us to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and to abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent. Together, these three are the traditional practices of Lent.”

Say: “They work together. Fasting without almsgiving is just a diet. Almsgiving without prayer is just philanthropy. Prayer without fasting and almsgiving can be empty words. A saying from the early Church says: ‘Prayer is good with fasting, and fasting with almsgiving.’ The point is a change of heart toward God and neighbor. We do them not to earn God’s love but because we are loved. And we ask for the grace to do it quietly, to please the Father.”
ask: What are the three practices in Matthew 6? (Almsgiving, prayer and fasting.)
Why should we do them in secret? (To please the Father, not to be admired.)
How do the three support each other? (Fasting makes room, almsgiving shares, prayer unites us to God.)
practice: Divide a sheet into three columns: Give, Pray, Fast.
Plan one specific action for each for the week. Make the almsgiving a secret act.
Make the fast something you can offer for a particular person or need.
Share only the prayer plan with a partner; keep the others secret.
script.close: Pray the Our Father slowly. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do your three promises quietly.”

tryit: Compare doing good to be seen with doing it in secret.
Plan a secret act.
Plan a fast for a person in need.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth was born in 1207, a princess of Hungary, and was married at fourteen to Louis, the ruler of Thuringia in Germany. They loved each other deeply and had three children. Elizabeth lived in a castle, but she spent her time and her wealth caring for the poor. She visited the sick, gave away food, and built a hospital below the castle.
In a famine, she opened the royal storehouses. Her courtiers were unhappy. According to a story, once, as she was carrying bread under her cloak to the poor, her husband stopped her and asked what she was carrying. When she opened her cloak, there were roses instead of bread.
Louis died on a crusade in 1227, when she was twenty. Her in-laws turned her out of the castle. She later became a lay Franciscan, built another hospital, and served the poor with her own hands. She died at twenty-four, in 1231. She is patron of charities.

lessons.title: Entering Jerusalem and the Last Supper
lessons.idea: Jesus entered Jerusalem as the humble king and then gave himself at the Last Supper. In the bread and wine he gave us his Body and Blood. This is the start of the Eucharist.
lessons.question: What do these events show?
lessons.activity: “Upper room” (30 min). Draw or build the setting of the Last Supper using Luke 22 and Passover customs. Mark the moments: washing of feet (John 13), the bread, the cup, “Do this in memory of me,” the new commandment. Connect to the Mass parts.
teach: The entry into Jerusalem fulfills Zechariah 9:9 (humble king on a donkey) and the crowds cry “Hosanna” (CCC 557–560). Palm Sunday begins Holy Week.
At the Last Supper Jesus instituted the Eucharist (CCC 1337–1340). “Do this in memory of me” gives the apostles and their successors the command.
The Last Supper was a Passover meal; the Eucharist is the new Passover (CCC 1340, 1363). John adds the foot washing and the new commandment (John 13:34).
On Holy Thursday the Church celebrates the institution of the Eucharist and the priesthood.
talk: What did Jesus do at the Last Supper?
How is the Eucharist both meal and sacrifice?
quiz: At the Last Supper Jesus gave…|His Body and Blood|A sign only|A parable|A sermon|0|Luke 22:19.
On Palm Sunday he rode…|A horse|A camel|A chariot|A donkey|3|Matthew 21.
“Do this in memory of me” establishes…|The Eucharist|Marriage|Ashes|Baptism|0|CCC 1341.
lessons.life: Read the Last Supper accounts side by side.
lessons.saint: Tarcisius: a boy who died carrying the Eucharist to the sick.
misc: “Palm Sunday is a happy day only.”
“The Last Supper was only a farewell dinner.”
lessons.mem: “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you knew it was your last night with your friends, what would you do?” Read Luke 22:7–20.
lessons.assess: Ask students to retell the Last Supper and explain two ways it connects to the Mass.

script.open: Say, “Imagine you know this is the last meal you will have with your closest friends. What would you say? What would you give them?” Take responses.
teach: Read Matthew 21:1-11 in summary. Say: “Jesus entered Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble king. The crowd laid down cloaks and palm branches and cried, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David!’ They expected a political king. A few days later, some of them would cry ‘Crucify him.’ We remember this on Palm Sunday, and begin Holy Week.”

Read Luke 22:7-20. Say: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread, Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the Passover. At the meal, Jesus ‘took bread, and when he had given thanks he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And likewise the cup after supper, saying, “This cup which is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.”’ At the Passover, Israel remembered the lamb whose blood saved them. Now Jesus is the Lamb, and the meal is the new Passover.”

Say: “At this supper, Jesus did several things. He instituted the Eucharist: his body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine. He instituted the priesthood: ‘Do this’ gave the apostles the power to do it. He washed their feet (John 13), giving the example of service. He gave the new commandment: ‘Love one another as I have loved you.’ He prayed for unity (John 17). Then he went to the Garden. We celebrate this on Holy Thursday. Every Mass makes present again this Supper and the sacrifice it anticipates.”
ask: What did Jesus do with the bread and cup? (Blessed, broke and gave; said this is my body and blood.)
What command did he give the apostles? (Do this in memory of me.)
What was Jesus’ example of service at the Supper? (He washed the disciples’ feet.)
practice: Draw two columns: the Passover meal and the Last Supper.
Fill in rows: the lamb / Jesus; unleavened bread / his body; the cup / his blood; the memorial / the Eucharist.
Underline what Jesus changed.
Write the words of Luke 22:19-20 from memory, as best you can.
script.close: Pray the Anima Christi or: “Jesus, I adore you in the Eucharist.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank an altar server or a priest.”

tryit: Compare the Passover and the Last Supper.
Mark what Jesus changed.
Write the words of institution.
lessons.saintStory:
Tarcisius lived in Rome in the third century, in a time when Christians were persecuted and the Mass was celebrated secretly. According to the old account, he was a young acolyte, a boy who served at the altar. One day the priest needed a messenger to carry the Eucharist to some Christians in prison who were awaiting execution. Tarcisius volunteered.
He carried the Blessed Sacrament wrapped in cloth, hidden against his chest. On the way, a group of boys saw him and asked what he was holding. He refused to show them. They knew he was a Christian, and began to beat him with sticks and stones. He held the Eucharist tightly and would not let go. A soldier who was a Christian came and drove them away, but Tarcisius was dying. He was carried back to the Christians, and died. The Host was found undamaged.
He is patron of altar servers. His story shows how much the early Christians valued the Eucharist.

lessons.title: Gethsemane, trial, cross
lessons.idea: In Gethsemane Jesus prayed in agony; he was arrested, tried, scourged and crucified. He freely accepted the Father’s will. The Passion shows both the depth of human sin and of God’s love.
lessons.question: Who is responsible?
lessons.activity: “Passion in parts” (35 min). Read Luke 22–23 in scenes with roles. After each scene, freeze and write a one-line reflection (“What does this show about Jesus? About us?”). Close with a few minutes of silence.
teach: In Gethsemane Jesus entrusts himself to the Father: “Not my will but yours” (Luke 22:42). His agony shows his humanity and obedience (CCC 612).
The trials before the Sanhedrin and Pilate show injustice. The responsibility is not on one people: all sinners are the cause (CCC 597–598).
On the Cross he forgives (“Father, forgive them”), promises paradise to the thief, and entrusts his mother (Luke 23:34, 43; John 19:26–27).
Treat the Passion reverently. Keep clear that his death was a free act of love (CCC 609).
talk: What do we learn from his words?
quiz: Jesus prayed in…|Gethsemane|Capernaum|Cana|Bethany|0|Luke 22:39-46.
His death was…|Accidental|A defeat|Unplanned|Freely accepted|3|CCC 609.
All sinners…|Are innocent|Share responsibility|Cannot be forgiven|Don’t matter|1|CCC 598.
lessons.life: Read the Passion in Luke.
lessons.saint: Veronica: the woman who, tradition says, wiped the face of Jesus on the way to Calvary.
misc: “The Jews are responsible for Jesus’ death.”
“Jesus did not know what would happen.”
lessons.mem: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 22:39–46. Ask: “Why would Jesus ask the disciples to stay awake?” Jesus is truly human and needs companions.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name key moments and explain what each shows about Jesus’ freedom and love.

script.open: Be silent for a moment. Then say quietly, “We are going to walk through the most important days of history. Please listen with respect.”
teach: Read Luke 22:39-46 and Mark 14:32-50 in summary. Say: “After the Supper, Jesus went to Gethsemane to pray. He took Peter, James and John, and said, ‘My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here and watch.’ He fell on the ground and prayed, ‘Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.’ He found them asleep. In his agony, his sweat became like drops of blood. Then Judas came with soldiers, and betrayed him with a kiss. The disciples fled.”

Say: “Jesus was taken to the high priest Caiaphas and the council, who accused him of blasphemy, since he said he was the Son of God. Peter denied him three times, then wept. In the morning Jesus was brought to Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate found no guilt in him, but afraid of the crowd, he had him scourged, and handed him over to be crucified. Soldiers mocked him with a crown of thorns. Jesus carried his cross to Golgotha, with Simon of Cyrene forced to help. There he was crucified between two criminals.”

Say: “On the cross, Jesus spoke seven times. ‘Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.’ To the good thief: ‘Today you will be with me in Paradise.’ To Mary and John: ‘Woman, behold your son… Behold your mother.’ ‘My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?’ (Psalm 22.) ‘I thirst.’ ‘It is finished.’ ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.’ Then he died. The curtain of the Temple was torn in two, the earth shook, and the centurion said, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God.’ Joseph of Arimathea laid him in a tomb. The Church remembers this on Good Friday.”
ask: What did Jesus pray in Gethsemane? (Not my will, but yours.)
Who denied Jesus? (Peter.)
What was Jesus’ first word on the cross? (Father, forgive them.)
practice: Prepare cards with the events of the Passion: Gethsemane, betrayal, Peter’s denial, trial before Pilate, scourging, carrying the cross, crucifixion, seven words, death, burial.
Put them in order.
Beside each, mark who was faithful and who failed.
Write one line of your own reflection: where would I have been?
script.close: Pray quietly: “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray the Stations of the Cross this Lent.”

tryit: Put the events of the Passion in order.
Mark where each person fails or is faithful.
Write one line for each station.
lessons.saintStory:
Veronica is not named in the Gospels. The Church honors her because of an old tradition that, as Jesus carried his cross through the streets of Jerusalem, a woman pushed through the crowd and soldiers, and offered him a cloth to wipe his face. When she looked at it later, the image of his face was on the cloth.
The name Veronica may come from the Latin and Greek words for “true image.” Whether or not the cloth story is literal, it holds a truth: one person among the crowd who showed compassion when everyone else failed. The sixth Station of the Cross remembers her.
The Gospels do name the women who stayed. Luke 23:27 says a great multitude of people followed Jesus, including women who mourned for him. John 19:25 says that Mary his mother, her sister, Mary of Clopas and Mary Magdalene stood by the cross. Many of the disciples fled, but these did not.

lessons.title: Why the Cross?
lessons.idea: Why did Jesus have to die? The New Testament offers images: ransom, sacrifice, expiation, reconciliation, the Suffering Servant bearing our sins. All point to love: “Greater love has no one than this.”
lessons.question: How does the Cross save?
lessons.activity: “Reflection and images” (30 min). Read Isaiah 53 and 1 Peter 2:24. Students list the images (ransom, sacrifice, healing, lamb). Choose the one that speaks most and write a reflection: “For me, the Cross means…” Share a few.
teach: Christ died “for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3; CCC 599–605). The Father did not demand the death of his Son as a cruel price; the Son freely offered himself in love (CCC 603–605).
Images: redemption (ransom), expiation, reconciliation, satisfaction (CCC 613–618). No single image exhausts the mystery.
“By his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24). The Cross is the sacrifice that Mass makes present (CCC 1366).
The Cross is also the way for us: “take up your cross” (CCC 618).
talk: How does the Cross shape our lives?
quiz: The Cross reveals…|God’s love|Roman law|God’s anger|Human power|0|CCC 604.
Christ died…|By accident|To impress|To scare us|For our sins|3|CCC 601.
“By his wounds we are…”|Healed|Warned|Led|Hurt|0|1 Peter 2:24.
lessons.life: Make the Sign of the Cross reverently.
lessons.saint: Paul of the Cross: a priest who taught people to meditate on the Passion.
misc: “God the Father punished Jesus because he was angry.”
lessons.mem: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” (John 15:13)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you owed a debt you couldn’t pay, and someone paid it, how would you feel?” Use as an image, not a full explanation.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain two images for the meaning of the Cross and avoid the misunderstanding that the Father is cruel.

script.open: Hold up a crucifix. Ask, “Why do Christians put a symbol of suffering in every church and home? Why not just a picture of the empty tomb?” Take answers.
teach: Read 1 Corinthians 1:22-24. Say: “Paul wrote, ‘We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.’ A crucified God was shocking. Crucifixion was a shameful form of execution. Yet Christians boasted in the cross, because there God’s love was fully shown. John 15:13: ‘Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.’”

Say: “The Catechism gives reasons why Jesus died. One: our sins. He died ‘for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures.’ (1 Corinthians 15:3) His death atones for sin, and reconciles us to the Father. Two: the Father’s love. ‘God so loved the world that he gave his only Son.’ (John 3:16) Three: it was freely chosen. Jesus said, ‘No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord.’ (John 10:18) Four: it was the sacrifice of the new covenant, the Lamb of God. The Mass makes this one sacrifice present.”

Say: “Jesus’ death does not cancel our suffering, but gives it meaning. Paul writes, ‘I am glad to suffer for your sake, and in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the Church.’ (Colossians 1:24) When we unite our troubles to the cross, they can bring blessing to others. Jesus said, ‘If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.’ (Luke 9:23) The cross is not the end. It leads to the Resurrection. We can say, ‘Hail, O Cross, our only hope.’”
ask: Why did Jesus die? (For our sins, out of the Father’s love, freely.)
What does 1 Corinthians 1 call the cross? (The power and wisdom of God.)
What happens when we unite our suffering to the cross? (It takes on meaning and can bless others.)
practice: Make four boxes: “For our sins,” “Out of love,” “Freely,” “As a sacrifice.”
In each, write a verse and a sentence in your own words.
Design a small cross card with a sentence on the back that you could give to a friend who is suffering.
Share one with a partner.
script.close: Pray the Sign of the Cross slowly with a crucifix in view. Send home: “Offer one small suffering this week for someone.”

tryit: Fill in the four reasons for the Cross.
Match each with a verse.
Explain it to a younger child.
lessons.saintStory:
Paul Danei was born in 1694 in northern Italy, and grew up in a family of merchants. As a young man he felt a strong call to remember the Passion of Jesus. After a vision, he put on a black tunic, and started to live as a hermit, praying and writing the rule for a new community.
