In 1720 he began to write down rules for a group of men devoted to the Passion. In 1741, the pope approved the Congregation of the Passion, the Passionists. Paul traveled through villages preaching missions, speaking with a quiet, strong conviction. He taught people to keep a simple image of the crucified Jesus before them. He told his priests to preach that the Passion is “the greatest and most overwhelming work of God’s love.”
He also said that suffering united to Christ’s becomes a gift. Paul died in 1775, at eighty-one. Today Passionists still preach the cross.

lessons.title: The empty tomb and appearances
lessons.idea: On the third day the tomb was empty and Jesus appeared to many: to Mary Magdalene, to the apostles, to Thomas, to the disciples at Emmaus. He rose in a real, glorified body.
lessons.question: What proof?
lessons.activity: “Compare the accounts” (30 min). Read the Resurrection narratives in Luke 24 and John 20. Make a table: who came to the tomb, who appeared, what was said, what Jesus did (ate, showed wounds). Note shared details and variations. Discuss Thomas.
teach: The empty tomb and the appearances are the foundation of the Church’s faith (CCC 639–644). Women were first witnesses, remarkable for the culture.

Jesus rose in a real body, not a resuscitation or a ghost: he ate (Luke 24:42–43) and bore wounds (John 20:27), yet he passes through doors and is not at once recognized. His body is glorified (CCC 645–646).
Paul lists witnesses, including 500 at once (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The apostles were willing to suffer and die for what they proclaimed.
Handle “proofs” carefully: the Resurrection is historical and also beyond history (CCC 647).
quiz: The first witnesses were…|Priests|Women|Soldiers|Kings|1|John 20:1.
The risen Jesus…|Appeared to many|Was a dream|Appeared to none|Was a ghost|0|1 Corinthians 15:5-8.
The Resurrection is…|Symbolic|Bodily|Spiritual only|Imaginary|1|CCC 645.
lessons.life: Read the four Resurrection accounts.
lessons.saint: Mary Magdalene: the first witness of the risen Lord, sent to tell the apostles.
lessons.mem: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28)
lessons.hook: Say: “If something this big happened, what evidence would you expect?” (an empty tomb, eyewitnesses, changed lives). Introduce the accounts.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three appearances and explain what they show about the risen body.

script.open: Read aloud the first lines of John 20:1-10 in a quiet voice. Stop after ‘He saw and believed.’ Ask, “What do you think he saw in the tomb? What was left behind?”
teach: Read John 20:1-18. Say: “Mary Magdalene came to the tomb on Sunday morning and found it empty. Peter and John ran to see. John ‘saw and believed.’ Mary stayed, and Jesus appeared to her. He called her by name. Notice how she recognized him: not by his face, but by his voice. Then he gave her a mission: ‘Go to my brethren and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father.’ A woman, whose testimony counted for little in that culture, was the first witness and the first messenger of the Resurrection.”

Say: “The Gospels record many appearances of the risen Jesus. To the women at the tomb (Matthew 28:9). To Peter. To the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, who recognized him in the breaking of the bread (Luke 24). To the ten apostles in the upper room, where he showed his wounds and said, ‘Peace be with you.’ To Thomas a week later: ‘Put your finger here… Do not be faithless, but believing.’ Thomas said, ‘My Lord and my God!’ To the seven by the Sea of Galilee, where he cooked breakfast and asked Peter three times, ‘Do you love me?’ And to the eleven on the mountain in Galilee, where he sent them into all the world.”

Say: “Paul lists the witnesses: ‘He appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at one time, most of whom are still alive… Last of all he appeared to me.’ (1 Corinthians 15:5-8) This was written within about twenty-five years of the event. The risen Jesus has a real body that can be touched and eats, yet can pass through doors. It is a glorified body. The disciples were changed from fearful men to fearless witnesses, willing to die for what they had seen.”
ask: Who was first to see the risen Jesus? (Mary Magdalene.)
How did she recognize him? (He called her by name.)
What did Jesus show Thomas? (His wounds.)
practice: Make a chart of appearances: who, where, what Jesus said, what happened next.
Use John 20, Luke 24, John 21 and Matthew 28.
Circle the one that speaks to you most.
Write what Jesus might say if he called your name.
script.close: Pray: “My Lord and my God.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Greet people with ‘Christ is risen!’ at Easter.”

tryit: Compare the Gospel accounts of the empty tomb.
List who found it and who saw the Lord.
Say what each person did next.
lessons.saintStory:
Mary Magdalene was from Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her. She followed Jesus and supported his ministry. She stood at the cross with Mary his mother and John, and saw where he was laid.
On the first day of the week, early in the morning, while it was still dark, she went to the tomb and found the stone rolled away. She ran to tell Peter and John, who came and saw the burial cloths. They went home, but Mary stayed outside, weeping. She looked in and saw two angels. “Woman, why are you weeping?” She turned and saw Jesus, but did not recognize him, thinking he was the gardener. He said, “Mary.” She said, “Rabboni!” (Teacher).
Jesus said, “Go to my brethren and say to them…” and she went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord.” She is called the apostle to the apostles.

lessons.title: The meaning of the Resurrection
lessons.idea: The Resurrection confirms that Jesus is God and that his teaching is true. It accomplishes our justification and new life, and it promises our own resurrection. “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is in vain.”
lessons.question: Why central?
lessons.activity: “Creed statement” (25 min). Read 1 Corinthians 15:1–22 aloud. Students write a three-sentence creed on the Resurrection: what happened, what it proves, what it promises. Compare with the Creed’s words.
teach: Paul: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The Resurrection is the “crowning truth of our faith” (CCC 638).
It confirms Jesus’ divinity and teaching (CCC 651–653), accomplishes our justification and new life (CCC 654), and is the pledge of our own resurrection (CCC 655).
Sunday is the weekly Easter. The Easter Vigil is the “mother of all vigils.” Baptism is a sharing in Christ’s death and resurrection (Romans 6:4).
The Resurrection answers the problem of death. Death is not the last word.
talk: Why does Paul say faith is futile without it?
quiz: Without the Resurrection, faith is…|Still strong|Futile|Easy|Fine|1|1 Corinthians 15:14.
Christ is the…|Firstfruits|Last|Forgotten|Middle|0|1 Corinthians 15:20.
The Resurrection gives us…|Power|New life|Fame|Wealth|1|Romans 6:4.
lessons.life: Celebrate Sunday as little Easter.
lessons.saint: Paul: a persecutor who met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus.
lessons.mem: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” (1 Corinthians 15:20)
lessons.hook: Say: “Imagine a team that has been told it has already won.” The Resurrection is the sign that evil has lost.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain three effects of the Resurrection.

script.open: Write the line ‘If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile’ on the board. Give a minute of silence and ask, “What would change in your life if that were true? What would stay the same?”
teach: Read 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 and 12-20. Say: “Paul told the Corinthians what he had received: ‘Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day… and that he appeared.’ Then he said some Christians were saying there was no resurrection. ‘If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.’ Everything depends on the Resurrection. But, Paul says, ‘Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep.’”

Say: “The Resurrection is the heart of the Christian faith. Jesus rose with a real, glorified body. It is not a resuscitation like Lazarus, who died again, nor merely a spiritual survival or a symbol. The tomb was empty. The risen Jesus was recognized by his wounds, yet he was transformed. Many witnesses saw him. The disciples, who had hidden, preached boldly and many died for it. The Resurrection is both a historical event and a mystery of faith, beyond our experience.”

Say: “What does it mean for us? It confirms who Jesus is: the Son of God, as he said. It is the victory over sin and death. It gives us new life: in Baptism we are raised with Christ (Romans 6:4). It is the promise of our own resurrection; at the end, our bodies will rise. It gives us hope. As we say in the Creed: ‘I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.’ Sunday is the day of the Resurrection, the ‘Lord’s Day.’ Every Mass celebrates his Pasch, his Passover from death to life.”
ask: Why does Paul say the Resurrection matters? (Without it, our faith is in vain.)
What kind of body did the risen Jesus have? (A real, glorified body.)
What does Baptism mean in relation to the Resurrection? (We rise with Christ to new life.)
practice: Draw a large empty tomb in the center of a sheet.
Around it, write five effects of the Resurrection: Jesus is God; sin and death defeated; new life in Baptism; our own resurrection; hope.
Next to each, write a verse (Romans 1:4, 1 Corinthians 15:55, Romans 6:4, 1 Corinthians 15:20, 1 Peter 1:3).
Write one sentence: “Because Christ is risen, I…”
script.close: Pray: “Christ is risen! He is risen indeed! Alleluia!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Say ‘Alleluia’ in your morning prayer.”

tryit: Fill in why the Resurrection matters.
Link each effect to a verse.
Say what difference it makes in your life.
lessons.saintStory:
Saul of Tarsus was a Pharisee, educated in Jerusalem, who believed the Christians were a danger to Israel. He consented to the death of Stephen, and went from house to house arresting Christians. He then got letters to travel to Damascus to arrest more.
On the road, around noon, a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asked, “Who are you, Lord?” The voice said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” He was blind for three days. In Damascus, Ananias, a disciple, was afraid, but obeyed the Lord, laid hands on him, and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus has sent me that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Something like scales fell from his eyes. He was baptized.
Paul became the great missionary to the Gentiles, traveling thousands of miles. He wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile.”

lessons.title: Ascension and Pentecost
lessons.idea: Jesus ascended to the Father and sent the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. The apostles, filled with courage, began the Church’s mission “to the ends of the earth.”
lessons.question: What happens next?
lessons.activity: “Map the mission” (30 min). Using Acts 1:8 as outline (Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth), students plot the spread on a map: Pentecost, Samaria, Ethiopia, Antioch, Asia Minor, Greece, Rome. Add key people.
teach: The Ascension is Christ’s enthronement and the pledge of our own ascent (CCC 659–667). He remains with us through the Church and the sacraments.
At Pentecost the Spirit comes with wind and fire; the apostles speak in many languages and Peter preaches (Acts 2). The Church is “born” (CCC 731–732, 767).
The Church’s mission is universal: “Go and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). Acts shows the Spirit guiding it.
The Spirit is still active. Invite students to name where.
quiz: Jesus ascended…|Immediately|Forty days after Easter|On Good Friday|At Christmas|1|Acts 1:3.
Pentecost is…|Fifty days after Easter|Ten|Forty|Seven|0|Acts 2.
The Spirit empowers…|Fear|Revenge|Witness|Hiding|2|Acts 1:8.
lessons.life: Pray for the gift of the Spirit.
lessons.saint: Matthias: chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve.
lessons.mem: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses.” (Acts 1:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you do if your leader left and said, ‘Wait for a gift’?” Read Acts 1:6–11.
lessons.assess: Ask students to trace Acts 1:8 on a map and describe Pentecost.

script.open: Ask, “How would you feel if your best friend and teacher left and said, ‘Wait here’? What would you do while waiting?”
teach: Read Acts 1:1-11. Say: “For forty days after the Resurrection, Jesus appeared to the apostles and taught them about the Kingdom. He told them, ‘You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth.’ Then he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. Two men in white said, ‘This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.’ The Ascension is when Jesus returned to the Father in glory, with his human body. He now intercedes for us.”

Read Acts 2:1-13. Say: “On the day of Pentecost, fifty days after Easter, the disciples were all together. ‘Suddenly a sound came from heaven like the rush of a mighty wind… And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, distributed and resting on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues.’ Crowds from many nations heard them, each in their own language. Peter then preached, and about three thousand were baptized that day. The Church was born, as the Holy Spirit came to dwell in the Church.”

Say: “The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity. He is the ‘Lord and giver of life’ in the Creed. Jesus promised him as the Advocate, the Counselor, who would teach and remind them of all that he said (John 14:26). The Spirit gives the Church unity, holiness, and the power to witness. The apostles who had hidden in fear now preached boldly. Pentecost reverses Babel: the languages that divided now gather people. The Church celebrates Pentecost fifty days after Easter. Each of us receives the Spirit in Baptism and Confirmation.”
ask: What happened at the Ascension? (Jesus returned to the Father in glory.)
What happened at Pentecost? (The Holy Spirit came upon the apostles and the Church began to preach.)
How does Pentecost answer Babel? (The Spirit unites people of all languages.)
practice: Make a timeline: Resurrection, forty days of appearances, Ascension, nine days in prayer, Pentecost.
Mark the apostles’ mission (Acts 1:8) and how they changed after Pentecost.
Draw the symbols: wind and fire.
Write a prayer asking for the Holy Spirit.
script.close: Pray the Veni Creator or: “Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the Spirit’s gifts daily.”

tryit: Put the Ascension and Pentecost events in order.
Mark what the apostles were told to do.
Mark what the Spirit changed.
lessons.saintStory:
After Jesus ascended, the eleven apostles returned to Jerusalem, to the upper room, where they stayed together in prayer with Mary and the women. About one hundred and twenty believers were gathered. Peter stood up and said that, as the Scriptures said, someone else should take Judas’s place among them.
The man had to have been with them from the baptism of John to the Ascension, a witness of the Resurrection. Two were put forward: Joseph called Barsabbas, and Matthias. They prayed, “Lord, who knows the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen.” They cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias. He was added to the eleven.
We hear nothing more of him in the New Testament. Tradition says that he preached in Judea and farther away, and died as a martyr. He represents the Church’s continuity: the apostolic ministry continues through those chosen to follow.

lessons.title: Life in the first community
lessons.idea: The first Christians “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” They shared their goods, prayed in the Temple and at home, and grew day by day.
lessons.question: What marked them?
lessons.activity: “Compare with our parish” (25 min). Draw a four-part chart: teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers. In each, list what our parish does and one thing we could do better. Choose one for the class to try.
teach: Acts 2:42–47 and 4:32–35 describe a community of teaching, fellowship (koinonia), Eucharist and prayer (CCC 949, 2624–2625).
They shared goods voluntarily: the root of Catholic charity and the ideal of solidarity (CCC 952).
The pattern is the Mass: Word (teaching), communion, bread, prayer. Even then the Church had leaders: the apostles and deacons (Acts 6:1–6).
There were conflicts and failures (Ananias and Sapphira, Acts 5), a reminder that the Church is holy and made of sinners.
quiz: The early Christians devoted themselves to…|Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer|Wealth|War|Politics|0|Acts 2:42.
They shared…|Their goods|Only prayers|Nothing|Their houses only|0|Acts 2:44-45.
Koinonia means…|Competition|Communion|Commerce|Control|1|CCC 949.
lessons.life: Do something with the parish this month.
lessons.saint: Barnabas: the “son of encouragement,” who sold a field to help the poor.
lessons.mem: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would a team that really loved each other look like?” Read Acts 2:42–47.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name the four marks of the early community and compare them with the Mass.

script.open: Divide the class in two. One group lists what a good community needs. The other lists what ruins one. Compare the lists and look at what the first Christians in Acts did about both.
teach: Read Acts 2:42-47. Say: “‘And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of the bread and the prayers.’ Here is a portrait of the first Christian community in Jerusalem. Notice four things. The apostles’ teaching: they learned the faith. Fellowship: they shared life. The breaking of the bread: the Eucharist. The prayers: they prayed together, in the Temple and in homes. The Church today is still marked by these: doctrine, community, sacraments and prayer.”

Say: “They also shared their goods. ‘All who believed were together and had all things in common; and they sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to all, as any had need.’ This was voluntary, not forced. Ananias and Sapphira died after lying about a gift, which shows how seriously they took honesty in the community (Acts 5). The early Christians gave to the poor and cared for the widows. Seven deacons, including Stephen, were chosen to serve the poor (Acts 6).”

Say: “The first community also grew by witness. ‘Day by day the Lord added to their number those who were being saved.’ They were persecuted, but joyful. Peter and John were arrested for preaching, and said, ‘We must obey God rather than men.’ They rejoiced to suffer for the name. Antioch is where they were first called Christians. The Church is not only a building but the people. Our parish is meant to be like this: a family of faith who pray, learn, share and serve.”
ask: What are the four marks of the first community? (Teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers.)
How did they treat the poor? (They shared goods and had deacons serve the needy.)
Where were the disciples first called Christians? (Antioch.)
practice: Make four boxes: Teaching, Fellowship, Breaking of bread, Prayers.
In each, write the verse from Acts 2:42-47 and one way your parish does it.
Add one way you could contribute.
Share with a partner.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, make us one in heart and mind.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Encourage someone like Barnabas this week.”

tryit: List the four marks of the first community.
Match each to a verse.
Write how your parish does it today.
lessons.saintStory:
Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus whose given name was Joseph. The apostles called him Barnabas, which means “son of encouragement.” In the first days of the Church in Jerusalem, he sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, to be shared with the needy.
When Saul, the former persecutor, came to Jerusalem after his conversion, the disciples were afraid of him. Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how he had seen the Lord. Later Barnabas went to Antioch, where Greeks were converting, and he brought Saul to help. There the disciples were first called Christians.
Barnabas and Saul were sent on the first missionary journey. Later he and Paul disagreed over whether to take John Mark along, and they parted, with Barnabas taking Mark. This turned out well, as Mark later became Paul’s helper and wrote the Gospel.

lessons.title: Peter and Paul
lessons.idea: Peter, the rock, led the Church, opened it to Gentiles (Cornelius) and was the first Pope. Paul, once a persecutor, met Christ on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles, traveling the Mediterranean.
lessons.question: How did the Gospel spread?
lessons.activity: “Map Paul’s journeys” (30 min). Trace Paul’s three missionary journeys and voyage to Rome. Mark Damascus, Antioch, Philippi, Corinth, Ephesus, Athens, Rome. Add Peter’s story in Acts 10 (Cornelius) at Caesarea. Compare their roles.
teach: Jesus gave Peter the keys: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18–19; CCC 551–553). Peter leads the apostles and the Church and confirms his brethren (Luke 22:32).
In Acts 10 Peter baptizes the Gentile Cornelius after a vision and the Spirit’s coming, showing the Church is for all (CCC 849–856).
Paul’s conversion (Acts 9) shows grace transforming a persecutor. His journeys planted churches. Both Peter and Paul were martyred in Rome (around AD 64–67). The Church celebrates them on June 29.
The Pope today is the successor of Peter (CCC 882).
quiz: Paul met Christ on the road to…|Antioch|Jerusalem|Rome|Damascus|3|Acts 9.
Peter first preached to Gentiles in…|Rome|Caesarea|Athens|Corinth|1|Acts 10.
Paul’s mission was to the…|Soldiers|Priests|Gentiles|Romans only|2|Galatians 2:8.
lessons.life: Map Paul’s journeys.
lessons.saint: Peter and Paul: two very different apostles who died in Rome for the same Lord.
misc: “Peter was just one apostle among equals.”
lessons.mem: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who is the most unlikely person you can imagine becoming a great missionary?” Read Acts 9:1–19.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Peter’s role, Paul’s role and how they worked together.

script.open: Write “Peter” and “Paul” on the board. Ask the class to say what they remember about each. Fill in. Ask, “Which one do you think would be an easier friend? Which easier to follow?”
teach: Read Acts 2:14-41 and Acts 3 in summary. Say: “After Pentecost, Peter stood up and preached to the crowd. About three thousand were baptized. Soon after, Peter and John healed a lame man at the Temple gate. ‘I have no silver and gold, but I give you what I have; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.’ They were arrested and warned not to preach. They answered, ‘We cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.’ Peter was in prison but freed by an angel (Acts 12). He led the Church in Jerusalem and then went to Rome.”

Read Acts 9:1-19 and 13-14 in summary. Say: “Paul was converted on the road to Damascus. He then went on three missionary journeys: Cyprus, Galatia, Greece (Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth) and Ephesus. In each city he first went to the synagogue, then to the Gentiles. He preached in the Areopagus in Athens, spoke to kings, was beaten, stoned, shipwrecked and imprisoned. He wrote, ‘I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.’ (1 Corinthians 9:22) He was a tentmaker and supported himself.”

Say: “Peter and Paul were different: Peter was a fisherman with little schooling, Paul was educated; Peter was leader of the twelve, Paul was the apostle to the Gentiles. Peter had denied Jesus, and Paul had persecuted his followers. Both were forgiven and became the pillars of the Church. God does not use perfect people, but willing ones. Their cooperation shows that the Church has room for different gifts under one Lord. We invoke them together on June 29. In the Eucharistic Prayer we name them among the apostles.”
ask: Who preached on Pentecost? (Peter.)
Which apostle is called the apostle to the Gentiles? (Paul.)
How did God use their weaknesses? (Both were forgiven and became leaders.)
practice: Draw a chart with two columns: Peter and Paul.
Rows: background, weakness, conversion or call, mission, death.
Fill in from the lesson and Scripture.
At the bottom, write what each teaches you.
script.close: Pray the collect of June 29 or: “Holy Peter and Paul, pray for us.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look at the statues of Peter and Paul in your church.”

tryit: Compare Peter and Paul.
Mark their strengths and weaknesses.
Say how God used them.
lessons.saintStory:
Peter was a fisherman from Galilee, impulsive and warm. Jesus gave him the name Rock, and said, “On this rock I will build my Church.” He walked on water and sank, declared that Jesus was the Christ, and denied him three times. After the Resurrection, Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love me?” and told him, “Feed my sheep.” After Pentecost, Peter led the Church.
Paul was a scholar, a Pharisee and a Roman citizen from Tarsus, precise and fiery. After his conversion, he traveled across the Roman Empire, founded churches and wrote letters. The two did not always agree. At Antioch, Paul opposed Peter to his face, over whether Jewish Christians should eat with Gentile converts. They settled it, and at the Council of Jerusalem they agreed.
Both came to Rome. Tradition says that Peter was crucified under Nero, upside down at his own request because he did not feel worthy to die as Jesus did, and Paul, as a citizen, was beheaded. The Church celebrates their feast together on June 29.

lessons.title: The Council of Jerusalem
lessons.idea: When Gentile converts raised the question of circumcision, the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem (Acts 15). Led by Peter and James and guided by the Spirit, they decided: Gentiles need not follow the whole Law. This is the model for Church councils.
lessons.question: Who decides?
lessons.activity: “Role-play the council” (30 min). Assign roles: Pharisee believers, Paul and Barnabas, Peter, James, an observer. Act the debate and the decision. Then write the letter (Acts 15:23–29). Discuss how this relates to councils like Nicaea.
teach: The Council of Jerusalem (c. AD 49) settled whether Gentiles must be circumcised (Acts 15). It combined testimony, Scripture and decision (CCC 865, 880–892).
Peter speaks first and definitively; James proposes a pastoral solution; the whole group agrees. “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” shows the Church’s authority (CCC 882–892).
It is the first ecumenical-style council. The Church has held 21 councils, including Nicaea (325), Trent (1545) and Vatican II (1962).
The Church’s unity is lived through bishops with the Pope.
quiz: The first council was in…|Ephesus|Nicaea|Jerusalem|Rome|2|Acts 15.
The decision concerned…|The calendar|Gentile converts|Music|Taxes|1|Acts 15:19.
It said, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to…”|Paul|Rome|The king|Us|3|Acts 15:28.
lessons.life: Read Acts 15.
lessons.saint: James the Just: the leader of the Jerusalem church who helped settle the first dispute.
misc: “Everyone in the Church decides by vote.”
lessons.mem: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” (Acts 15:28)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How should a group settle a serious disagreement?” Read Acts 15:1–2 and the verdict in 15:28: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the question, who decided and how the decision was reached.

script.open: Stage a quick mock dispute: two sides disagree about a school rule. Let each side speak for one minute. Then ask the class, “Who decides, and how do you know the decision is fair?”
teach: Read Acts 15:1-35 in summary. Say: “Some Jewish Christians came to Antioch and taught, ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.’ Paul and Barnabas argued with them. This was a major crisis: was Christianity a branch of Judaism, or something for all nations? The Church met in Jerusalem. This is the first Church council. The apostles and elders gathered. There was much debate.”

Say: “Notice how they decided. They listened to each side. Peter said, ‘God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us… we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus.’ Paul and Barnabas told of the miracles among the Gentiles. James connected it with Scripture. They reached a decision, and wrote a letter: ‘It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us…’ The letter was carried to Antioch, and the people rejoiced. They made a decision under the guidance of the Spirit, with Peter and the apostles leading.”

Say: “This is a model for the Church. The Church has met in ecumenical councils, such as Nicaea, Trent and Vatican II, when the Pope and bishops gather to settle questions of faith and discipline. They decide with the Spirit’s guidance and Peter’s successor’s confirmation. The Church’s teaching doesn’t change in its core, but it develops and clarifies, as the Spirit leads the Church into all truth (John 16:13). The first council also teaches that salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus, not by works of the Law, and that the Church is for all nations.”
ask: What question did the Council of Jerusalem answer? (Whether Gentile converts must follow the Law of Moses.)
Who led the discussion? (Peter, with James and the apostles.)
How do councils decide today? (With the Pope and bishops, guided by the Spirit.)
practice: Act out the Council in a role-play: Peter, James, Paul, Barnabas, the men from Judea.
Students prepare their speeches from Acts 15.
After the debate, write a short letter in the council’s name giving the decision.
Compare it with Acts 15:28-29.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, guide your Church.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray for the Pope and bishops.”

tryit: Trace the steps of the Council of Jerusalem.
Mark who spoke and what was decided.
Say how the Church decides today.
lessons.saintStory:
James, called “the brother of the Lord” in the New Testament, was a relative of Jesus. In the Gospels, his relatives had been skeptical of Jesus. Paul lists him among those to whom the risen Jesus appeared. After that, James became a leader in the Jerusalem church, and was known as “the Just” for his devotion to prayer and the Law.
When Gentiles began to join the Church, a serious question arose: did they need to be circumcised and follow the whole Law of Moses? Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem with this question. Around the year 49, the apostles and elders gathered. After much discussion, Peter spoke, and then Paul and Barnabas told of the signs God had done among the Gentiles. Then James spoke, quoting the prophet Amos, and proposed that the Gentiles not be burdened.
The council wrote a letter: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.” According to tradition, James was martyred in Jerusalem in about AD 62.

lessons.title: Paul’s letters
lessons.idea: Paul’s letters explain what Jesus’ death and resurrection mean. In Romans he teaches that we are justified by grace through faith, a faith that works through love, and that the Spirit makes us God’s children.
lessons.question: What is justification?
lessons.activity: “Outline Romans” (30 min). Students outline chapters 5–8: justified by faith (5), dead to sin and alive in Christ (6), struggle with sin (7), life in the Spirit (8). For each, write a one-line summary and a key verse (5:8, 6:4, 7:24–25, 8:38–39).
teach: Justification is God’s gift: forgiveness and new life by grace through faith in Christ (CCC 1987–1995). It is not earned by works, yet faith “works through love” (Galatians 5:6; CCC 1814, 2010).
Catholic teaching: grace initiates, faith responds, and good works are the fruit and also meritorious by God’s grace (CCC 2006–2011). The Church affirms that Paul and James agree (James 2:24).
In Romans 8 Paul describes life in the Spirit: adoption as children, nothing can separate us from God’s love (CCC 1996–1999).
Avoid caricaturing Protestant views; the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999) shows convergence.
talk: How do faith and works relate?
quiz: Justification is…|Feeling good|Earning salvation|A law|Being made righteous by grace|3|CCC 1989.
Faith works through…|Money|Love|Fear|Pride|1|Galatians 5:6.
Nothing can separate us from…|Death|Debt|The love of Christ|Sin|2|Romans 8:39.
lessons.life: Memorize Romans 8:38–39.
lessons.saint: Phoebe: the woman who carried Paul’s letter to the Romans.
misc: “Catholics think you earn salvation by works.”
lessons.mem: “For I am sure that neither death nor life… will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38–39)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Can you earn a gift?” (No; then it’s a wage.) Read Romans 5:1–11 and Ephesians 2:8–9. Grace is a gift.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain justification by grace and the role of faith and works.

script.open: Ask, “When was the last time you got a real letter? Why do people write letters? What did Paul need to say that he couldn’t say in person?”
teach: Say: “Of the 27 books of the New Testament, 21 are letters, or epistles. Thirteen are attributed to Paul: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus and Philemon. Hebrews has traditionally been associated with him. Then there are the Catholic epistles by James, Peter, John and Jude. Paul wrote his letters to real communities, answering their problems, from about AD 50 to 65. They are the earliest New Testament writings.”

Say: “A typical letter has a pattern: a greeting (‘Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus… to the church of God at Corinth’), a thanksgiving, the main teaching, practical advice, and personal greetings and a blessing. Romans teaches that we are justified by faith in Jesus, not works of the Law. Corinthians deals with divisions, the Eucharist and love (chapter 13). Galatians defends freedom in Christ. Ephesians speaks about the Church as Christ’s body. Philippians is a letter of joy written from prison. Philemon asks a master to welcome back a runaway slave as a brother.”

Say: “Some things in Paul are hard to understand, as 2 Peter 3:16 admits. That’s why we read with the Church. Paul’s message is that God’s grace in Christ saves us, and faith works through love. He wrote, ‘For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not your own doing, it is the gift of God.’ (Ephesians 2:8) Yet he also wrote, ‘Faith working through love.’ (Galatians 5:6) The Catholic teaching joins both: we are saved by grace, received by faith, and shown by good works. The letters are read in every Mass as the second reading.”
ask: How many New Testament books are letters? (21.)
Name two letters of Paul. (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, etc.)
What does Paul say saves us? (God’s grace, received through faith working through love.)
practice: Read the opening of Philippians 1:1-11 together.
Mark the greeting, the thanksgiving, and the prayer.
Write a short letter to a friend or a younger student in the same pattern: greeting, thanks, message, blessing.
Read one to a partner.
script.close: Pray Philippians 1:9-11 together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Write a note of encouragement to someone.”

tryit: Read the opening of a Pauline letter.
Find the greeting, thanks, message and closing.
Write a short letter in the same pattern.
lessons.saintStory:
Phoebe is named only once, in Paul’s letter to the Romans. Paul wrote: “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a deaconess of the church at Cenchreae, that you may receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may require from you, for she has been a helper of many and of myself as well.”
Cenchreae was a port near Corinth. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth in about AD 57. Most scholars think Phoebe carried the letter to Rome, a long sea journey. Whoever carried a letter in those days also read it aloud to the community and answered questions about it. So Phoebe was likely the first person to read Romans to the Church in Rome, and the first to explain it.
She shows that behind every letter is a person who carried it, and that the Church has always depended on helpers.

lessons.title: Living the Christian life
lessons.idea: The letters give practical guidance for Christian life: “put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving.” Paul calls the Church to unity, holiness, and love in family and community.
lessons.question: What are the “clothes” of a Christian?
lessons.activity: “Clothing list” (25 min). Students make a “wardrobe of virtues” from Colossians 3 and Ephesians 4–6 (compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiveness, love, peace, gratitude). For each write a real situation at school or home where they will “put it on.”
teach: Paul’s letters combine doctrine and morality: “you have put off the old nature… and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10). Baptism changes how we live.
He teaches about the Church (Ephesians 4:1–6: one body, one Spirit, one Lord) and about households (Ephesians 5–6), always “in Christ.”
The fruits of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23) are the sign of this life (CCC 1832).
Note that some texts (e.g., on slaves or women) have been misused. The Church reads them in light of the whole Gospel and human dignity (CCC 1935).
talk: What does it mean to “put on” Christ?
quiz: Put on…|Pride|Compassion|Anger|Envy|1|Colossians 3:12.
Above all, put on…|Love|Silence|Fear|Money|0|Colossians 3:14.
Do everything in the name of…|Rome|The world|The Lord Jesus|Self|2|Colossians 3:17.
lessons.life: Choose one virtue from Colossians 3 each day.
lessons.saint: Timothy: a young leader whom Paul told, “Let no one despise your youth.”
misc: “Christian life is only about avoiding sin.”
lessons.mem: “Above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.” (Colossians 3:14)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If you were writing a letter to your parish about how to treat each other, what would you say?” Read Colossians 3:12–17.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name five virtues Paul lists and give an example for each.

script.open: Hand out two lists, ‘works of the flesh’ and ‘fruit of the Spirit,’ from Galatians 5, with the labels hidden. Ask students to sort the words into two groups, then reveal Paul’s headings.
teach: Read Galatians 5:16-26. Say: “Paul describes a struggle: ‘The desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh.’ By ‘flesh’ he means our fallen nature, not our body. The works of the flesh are obvious: immorality, impurity, idolatry, enmity, strife, jealousy, anger, selfishness, envy, drunkenness. The fruit of the Spirit is ‘love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.’ A fruit is something that grows naturally from a healthy tree. We do not manufacture it; the Spirit produces it as we stay united with Christ.”

Read Romans 12:1-21. Say: “Paul gives a summary of Christian life. ‘Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.’ ‘Do not be conformed to this world but be transformed by the renewal of your mind.’ Everyone has different gifts, as members of one body. Then: ‘Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer. Bless those who persecute you. Live in harmony. Do not repay evil for evil. If your enemy is hungry, feed him. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.’”

Read 1 Corinthians 13. Say: “The greatest is love. Paul said, if I speak in tongues but have not love, I am a noisy gong. Love is patient and kind; it is not jealous or boastful or arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends. Faith, hope and love abide; the greatest of these is love. Each of the theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, are gifts of God. The Christian life is a life of love, lived by the Spirit.”
ask: What are the fruits of the Spirit? (Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.)
What does Paul mean by ‘flesh’? (Our fallen nature, not the body.)
Which virtue is the greatest? (Love.)
practice: Draw a tree with nine fruits labeled.
Beside each, rate yourself honestly from 1 to 5.
Pick the fruit you most want to grow, and write one action that would help.
Write 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 with your own name in place of “love.”
script.close: Pray: “Come, Holy Spirit, grow your fruit in me.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Practice your chosen fruit all week.”

tryit: List the fruits of the Spirit and the works of the flesh.
Mark where you are strong or weak.
Choose one fruit to grow.
lessons.saintStory:
Timothy was a young man from Lystra, in what is now Turkey. His mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers, and Paul praised the faith that first lived in them. Timothy had known the Scriptures from childhood. Paul met him on his second journey and took him as a companion. He became Paul’s close co-worker and friend, “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord.”
Paul sent Timothy on delicate missions to Corinth, Thessalonica and Philippi, and in the end left him in charge of the church at Ephesus. He wrote him two letters to guide him. “Let no one despise your youth, but set the believers an example in speech and conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” Paul also told him to stir up the gift of God that was in him through the laying on of hands.
Tradition says Timothy was the first bishop of Ephesus and was killed by a mob around AD 97.

lessons.title: Revelation: hope for the end
lessons.idea: Revelation unveils Christ’s victory and the new creation. Its visions, full of symbols from the Old Testament, comfort persecuted Christians and show the heavenly liturgy. It ends with God dwelling among us and “Come, Lord Jesus!”
lessons.question: What is the message of hope?
lessons.activity: “Final chapters” study (30 min). Read Revelation 21–22. Students list images (new Jerusalem, river of life, tree of life, no temple, light of the Lamb) and trace each to the Old Testament (Genesis, Ezekiel, Isaiah). Then link to the Mass (Holy, Holy, Holy; the Lamb of God).
teach: Revelation is apocalyptic literature, written to encourage the persecuted: the Lamb has conquered (CCC 1042–1050). Its symbols (numbers, beasts, colors) are not a timetable for the end.
The heavenly liturgy (Revelation 4–5) is the model of the Mass; we join the angels and saints in worship (CCC 1137–1139). The “new Jerusalem” is the Church in glory.
The final prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” (22:20) is the cry of the Church; “Maranatha” is prayed in the Eucharist (CCC 1130).
Warn gently against date-setting and fear-based interpretations. The Church teaches that no one knows the day or hour (CCC 673).
quiz: Revelation ends with…|Judgment only|Defeat|Silence|New Jerusalem|3|Revelation 21.
Its main message is…|Christ wins|Doom|Fear|Politics|0|CCC 1042.
“Behold, I make all things…”|New|Lost|Old|Dark|0|Revelation 21:5.
lessons.life: Read Revelation 21–22 aloud.
lessons.saint: John: the beloved disciple who stood at the cross and saw heaven opened.
lessons.mem: “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5)
lessons.hook: Read Revelation 21:1–5 aloud. Ask: “What is missing in that city?” (tears, death, mourning, pain). Hope is the point of the book.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Revelation’s purpose and give two images of the new creation.

script.open: Show a famous painting of the Lamb of God from the Ghent Altarpiece or a similar image. Give a minute of silent looking. Ask, “What details seem strange? What might they mean?”
teach: Say: “The Book of Revelation, or the Apocalypse, was written by John, probably about AD 95, to Christians under persecution by the Roman Emperor. It uses symbols and visions typical of a style called apocalyptic. ‘Apocalypse’ means ‘unveiling’: it reveals what is really happening behind events. It is not a code for predicting dates. It is a message of hope: Christ has won, and will win. The book begins with ‘Revelation of Jesus Christ’ and letters to seven churches.”

Say: “The symbols are drawn from the Old Testament. The Lamb who was slain, standing, is Christ (Revelation 5). The number seven means completeness; 666, a number of imperfect pride, probably refers to Rome’s emperor. The beast stands for the empire that persecutes and demands worship. The woman clothed with the sun (Revelation 12) is Israel and the Church, and also Mary. The great harlot, Babylon, is Rome and every society that is against God. White robes, palms and the book of life are signs of the faithful. The dragon is Satan. There are battles, but the Lamb conquers.”

Say: “Revelation is full of liturgy. The heavenly worship has an altar, incense, a Lamb, and the song ‘Holy, holy, holy.’ The Mass joins this: when we sing the Sanctus and the Lamb of God, we join the angels. The book ends with a vision of the new heaven and new earth (chapters 21-22): ‘Behold, I make all things new.’ God wipes away every tear. ‘Death shall be no more.’ The last words of the Bible are a prayer: ‘Come, Lord Jesus!’ The Church prays this every Advent. We live in hope.”
ask: What does ‘apocalypse’ mean? (Unveiling.)
Who is the Lamb in Revelation? (Jesus.)
What are the last words of the Bible? (Come, Lord Jesus!)
practice: Make a chart of Revelation’s images: Lamb, dragon, beast, woman clothed with the sun, white robes, new Jerusalem.
Beside each, write what it stands for.
Find two places in the Mass that match Revelation (Holy, Holy, Holy; Lamb of God).
Write a short message of hope you could send to a person who is suffering.
script.close: Pray: “Come, Lord Jesus!” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Read Revelation 21:1-5 with your family.”

tryit: Match the symbols of Revelation to their meaning.
Find the Mass parallels.
Write the message of hope.
lessons.saintStory:
John was a fisherman with his brother James and father Zebedee. Jesus called them from the nets, and nicknamed them the “sons of thunder.” John became one of the three closest to Jesus. At the Last Supper, he leaned on Jesus’ chest. At the cross, he alone of the Twelve stood by with Mary and the women, and Jesus gave Mary to him as his mother.
After the Resurrection, he was the first to recognize Jesus at the Sea of Galilee. “It is the Lord!” He and Peter led the early Church. In his old age, he lived in Ephesus. Tradition says that he wrote the Gospel, three letters and the book of Revelation, and he lived to be the last of the apostles. He was exiled to the island of Patmos, “on account of the word of God.”
There he saw visions of heaven, and wrote them down for the seven churches in Asia. Tradition says that as an old man, he kept repeating to his people, “Little children, love one another.”

units.title: Honoring family and respecting life
units.eq: How does love shape our family and our respect for each person?

lessons.title: Honor your father and mother
lessons.idea: The fourth commandment asks children to honor and obey parents, and asks parents and leaders to serve those in their care. The family is the first school of love, and honor continues as parents age.
lessons.question: What does it mean to honor parents?
lessons.activity: Write a letter of thanks to a parent, grandparent or guardian. List ways to honor adults who care for you at home, in school and in the parish.
teach: The fourth commandment: “Honor your father and mother” (CCC 2196–2200). It is the first with a promise (Ephesians 6:2). Honor includes respect, gratitude, obedience while young and care when they are old (CCC 2214–2220).
Parents have duties: to love, teach, protect and respect their children’s freedom (CCC 2221–2231). The family is a “domestic church” (CCC 2204–2206).
Obedience has limits: we obey God before any human command, and abuse is never right (CCC 2242). If someone is being harmed, they should tell a trusted adult.
Public authorities also have duties to serve the common good (CCC 2234–2246).
talk: What does honoring a parent look like when you disagree?
How can you help your family this week?
Who should you tell if someone is being hurt?
quiz: The fourth commandment says to…|Not lie|Rest on Sunday|Honor your father and mother|Not steal|2|Exodus 20:12.
The family is called the…|School|Business|Town|Domestic church|3|CCC 2204.
We must obey God…|After everyone else|Never|Only at church|Before any human command|3|CCC 2242.
lessons.life: Do one unrequested job at home and thank a parent or guardian in words.
lessons.saint: Tobias: a son who cared for his blind father and journeyed with an angel.
lessons.mem: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land.” (Exodus 20:12)
lessons.hook: Ask students to name one thing a family member did for them this week. Say that honoring is first noticing.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain honor and two ways they will show it.

script.open: Ask, “What is one thing your parent or guardian does for you that you never say thank you for?” Take a few answers.
teach: Read Exodus 20:12 and Ephesians 6:1-4. Say: “‘Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the Lord your God gives you.’ This is the fourth commandment, and the first that comes with a promise. Paul: ‘Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.’ And fathers, ‘do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.’ The commandment goes both ways. Children owe respect, gratitude, obedience and care in old age. Parents owe love, care, education, and a good example.”

Say: “The family is the first school of faith and the ‘domestic church.’ A child learns to pray, to love, to forgive and to serve at home. Jesus himself ‘was obedient to them.’ (Luke 2:51) Obedience has limits: we obey parents unless they ask us to do wrong. Honor continues as we grow up: caring for aging parents is a duty. Jesus condemned those who got out of caring for their parents by calling their money ‘Corban,’ dedicated to God (Mark 7:10-13).”

Say: “The fourth commandment also extends to others in authority: teachers, employers, officers, civic leaders. We owe them respect and obedience when they lawfully act. They in turn have a duty to serve, not dominate. Citizens should pay taxes, vote, defend their country, and do their part for the common good. We must never obey orders that are against God’s law: ‘We must obey God rather than men.’ The Church is also a family, and we honor our spiritual fathers, and Mary, our mother.”
ask: Which commandment is about family? (The fourth.)
What do parents owe their children? (Love, care, education, good example.)
When must we not obey? (When asked to do something against God’s law.)
practice: Make two columns: “What children owe” and “What parents owe.”
Add a third for teachers and other authorities.
Plan one specific act of honor for a parent or guardian, such as writing a thank-you note, doing a chore without being asked, or listening.
Do it this week.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, bless my family.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Thank a parent or grandparent for something specific.”

tryit: List what children owe parents and what parents owe children.
Add duties to others in authority.
Plan one concrete act of honor.
lessons.saintStory:
Tobit was a faithful Jew exiled in Nineveh, who gave alms and buried the dead. One night, after burying a man, he slept outside, and bird droppings fell in his eyes and made him blind. His family fell into poverty. Tobit prayed to die, but then remembered that he had left money in a distant city.
He sent his son Tobias to get it, and told him, “Honor your mother all the days of your life. You must not forget how many dangers she endured for you in her womb.” Tobias set out with a guide, who was really the angel Raphael. On the way, a fish tried to swallow Tobias. At Raphael’s advice, he kept its heart, liver and gall. In a distant city, he married Sarah, and returned.
Tobias used the fish’s gall on his father’s eyes, and Tobit could see again. Raphael revealed himself: “I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand before the Lord.” The book of Tobit shows a family where parents and children honored each other.

lessons.title: You shall not kill: the gift of every life
lessons.idea: Every life is a gift from God, from conception to natural death. The fifth commandment forbids murder and calls us to protect life, make peace, avoid revenge and care for our health and safety.
lessons.question: How do we respect every life?
lessons.activity: Make a “life poster” showing ways to protect and cherish life at every age: care for babies, the sick, the elderly, creation. Add one act of peacemaking.
teach: Human life is sacred because each person is made in God’s image (CCC 2258–2262). The commandment forbids killing the innocent and teaches us to settle anger peacefully (CCC 2302–2306; Matthew 5:21–22).
It covers bullying, hatred, scandal, drugs, reckless risk and neglect of our health (CCC 2284–2291). Taking care of our body is a duty.
Jesus calls us to be peacemakers (CCC 2304–2305). Revenge is forbidden; forgiveness is the way.
Treat gently: students may have experienced loss or violence. Provide resources.
talk: What does it mean that all people are made in God’s image?
Who is easy to overlook when it comes to respect?
quiz: Life is sacred because…|It is long|We say so|It is useful|Made in God’s image|3|CCC 2258.
Jesus teaches that anger…|Can lead to sin and needs peace|Is a gift|Is never felt|Is always fine|0|Matthew 5:22.
A peacemaker is…|Alone|Weak|Silly|Blessed|3|Matthew 5:9.
lessons.life: Make peace with someone you have argued with, and pray for someone who is sick.
lessons.saint: Gianna Beretta Molla: a doctor and mother who chose her child’s life.
misc: “The fifth commandment is only about murder.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” (Matthew 5:9)
lessons.hook: Ask: “How can words or actions hurt someone without touching them?” List answers and connect to anger.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the fifth commandment and name three ways to protect life.

script.open: Light a candle and let it burn in silence for thirty seconds. Say, “A flame can be passed without losing anything. Life is like this too: given, not made by us.” Then ask students to name something they received as a gift.
teach: Read Genesis 1:27, Psalm 139:13-16 and Jeremiah 1:5. Say: “‘God created man in his own image.’ ‘You formed my inmost being; you knit me in my mother’s womb.’ ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.’ Every human life is a gift from God, made in his image and loved by him from the very beginning. Human life is sacred, from conception until natural death. This is the basis for the fifth commandment: ‘You shall not kill.’ (Exodus 20:13) Only God is the master of life.”

Say: “What does the commandment forbid? Murder, the intentional killing of an innocent person. Abortion, the direct killing of an unborn child; the Church teaches that this is a grave sin, and those who procure it are excommunicated. Euthanasia, intentionally ending the life of the sick, the elderly or the dying. Suicide, which is against love of self and God; the Church prays for those who die this way and entrusts them to God’s mercy. Also forbidden: harm to the body, such as drug abuse, and the denial of respect to others, such as hatred or scandal.”

Say: “There are also positive duties. We must care for the sick and dying. We should respect the weak. We are to work for peace. The Church allows self-defense, and just war under strict conditions, since protecting life is important. She opposes the death penalty where other means can protect society. Jesus goes deeper: anger and contempt are where killing begins. We are called to reconcile and forgive. The Church supports mothers in need, adoption and care for those who suffered after abortion, including God’s mercy through Confession. Every life is a gift. We pray and work for a culture of life.”
ask: Why is human life sacred? (We are made in God’s image and loved from the beginning.)
What does the fifth commandment forbid? (Murder, abortion, euthanasia, suicide.)
What are positive duties? (Care for the sick, respect the weak, work for peace.)
practice: Read Psalm 139:13-16 aloud in a circle.
Write a list: why every life has dignity (made in God’s image, loved by God, redeemed by Christ, unique).
Add ways to protect life in your community: pregnancy centers, visiting the elderly, supporting people in need.
Write a short prayer for the unborn, the sick and the dying.
script.close: Pray: “Lord, you are the author of life. Protect every person.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray a decade of the Rosary for life.”

tryit: Read Psalm 139:13-16.
List why every life has dignity.
Write a prayer for the unborn.
lessons.saintStory:
Gianna Beretta was born in Italy in 1922, one of thirteen children. She became a doctor, specializing in children, and worked among mothers and babies and the poor. She loved mountaineering, skiing and music. She married Pietro Molla in 1955, and they had three children.
In 1961, while pregnant with their fourth child, Gianna was found to have a tumor on her uterus. The doctors offered options, including one that would save her life but end the baby’s. As a doctor, she understood the risk. She chose the operation that removed the tumor while preserving the baby, and she asked her family, “If you must decide between me and the child, do not hesitate: choose the child. I insist on it. Save the baby.”
Gianna Emanuela was born on April 21, 1962, healthy. A week later, Gianna died of complications. She was thirty-nine. She was named a saint in 2004, and her daughter, a doctor too, attended the ceremony.

lessons.title: Faithful love: purity and the dignity of the body
lessons.idea: The sixth commandment asks us to respect our bodies and the bodies of others. Chastity is the virtue that helps us love well. God made the body good, and the gift of sexuality belongs to marriage.
lessons.question: What does it mean that my body is a gift?
lessons.activity: Use age-appropriate materials from your parish or school for this lesson, with parents informed. Work with students to write a “respect pledge” for friendships, language and media.
teach: God made us male and female, equal in dignity, and the body is good (Genesis 1:27; CCC 2331–2336). We are a unity of body and soul.
Chastity is the integration of sexuality into the whole person (CCC 2337–2347). Everyone is called to chastity according to their state of life (CCC 2348–2350).
Modesty protects the intimacy of the person (CCC 2521–2524). We respect others’ boundaries and say no to anything that treats people as objects.
Follow your diocese’s guidelines and inform parents. Keep language age-appropriate and dignified. Never ask students for personal disclosures.
talk: What does respect look like with friends and online?
Who are trusted adults you can talk to?
Why is it good to have boundaries?
quiz: The body is…|A good gift from God|Bad|Only a machine|Unimportant|0|CCC 2332.
Chastity is…|Fear|Integration of sexuality in the person|Silence|Hiding|1|CCC 2337.
Everyone is called to…|Silence|Marriage|Nothing|Chastity in their state of life|3|CCC 2348.
lessons.life: Choose one media habit or friendship boundary to protect your dignity and others’.
lessons.saint: Agnes of Rome: a girl of about thirteen who chose Christ above everything.
misc: “The Church thinks the body is bad.”
lessons.mem: “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians 6:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does it mean to treat a gift with care?” Hold up a wrapped gift and connect to the body.
lessons.assess: Ask students to define chastity and name one practical boundary.

script.open: Say calmly, “This is a topic that matters and that can feel awkward. We will be respectful and plain.” Then write ‘gift’ on the board and ask students what the word means, and what it asks of the person who receives one.
teach: Read 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. Say: “‘Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God? You are not your own; you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.’ Our bodies are not objects. They are part of who we are, made by God, redeemed by Christ, and called to the resurrection. In Baptism, we became temples of the Holy Spirit. The body is good, and sexuality is a gift of God.”

Say: “God made us male and female (Genesis 1:27). Sexuality is meant for love and for life, within marriage. The sixth commandment, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ and the ninth, ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,’ protect the gift. The virtue that governs it is chastity: integrating our sexuality so that we can give ourselves in love. Everyone is called to chastity according to their state of life: single persons and children practice purity in thought, word and deed; married couples practice fidelity; priests and religious live celibacy. Chastity is not repression, but self-mastery that frees us to love.”

Say: “Today it is not easy. The culture promotes the opposite: pornography, immodesty, hooking up, treating people as objects. The Church teaches that pornography harms those who view it and those who are exploited. Impurity can be forgiven in Confession, and God’s mercy is greater than any sin. Practical help: pray, receive the sacraments, choose good friends, be modest in dress and speech, avoid occasions of sin, guard the eyes and the screen, talk to a trusted adult. Mary is our model of purity. Jesus said, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’”
ask: What is chastity? (Integrating our sexuality so we can give ourselves in love according to our state.)
Why is the body sacred? (It is a temple of the Holy Spirit.)
What helps us live purity? (Prayer, sacraments, good friends, modesty, guarding the eyes, talking to a trusted adult.)
practice: On cards write short situations (for example, a friend shares an inappropriate picture; someone makes a joke about another’s body; a friend pressures another to look at something online).
In pairs, discuss what a chaste, respectful response would be.
Write a short personal commitment: “I will protect my purity by…”
Keep it private, or share with a parent.
script.close: Pray the Hail Mary for purity. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Talk with a trusted adult about any questions you have.”

tryit: Sort cases into respect and disrespect.
Say what the body is for.
Write a personal commitment.
lessons.saintStory:
Agnes lived in Rome around the year 300. She was about thirteen, from a noble family, and a Christian. Many young men admired her and wished to marry her, but she told them that she belonged to Christ alone. One young man, the son of a Roman official, was refused, and in his anger he accused her of being a Christian.
The persecution under Diocletian was at its worst. The governor tried to persuade her with threats and promises, but she would not offer sacrifice to the idols. Accounts of her death vary, but she was executed for her faith, probably by the sword. She was one of the first saints named in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Her name means “pure,” and in Latin it sounds like agnus, “lamb.”
Two months after her death, her parents prayed at her tomb, and she was said to have appeared to them in a vision. Agnes shows that purity is a strength, a gift for love.
